articles.headline: Nobel de physique 2026 : Francis Halzen récompensé pour avoir ouvert une nouvelle fenêtre sur l’Univers
articles.dek: News · 7 octobre 2026
articles.summary: Le Nobel de physique 2026 récompense Francis Halzen, père de l’observatoire IceCube enfoui dans la glace antarctique, qui a détecté des neutrinos venus d’au-delà du Système solaire.

cover.alt: Le bâtiment de l’observatoire IceCube sur la glace du pôle Sud
cover.credit: Photo: Christopher Michel / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.text: Le prix Nobel de physique 2026 a été attribué au physicien belgo-américain Francis Halzen pour ses contributions décisives à l’observatoire de neutrinos IceCube et à la découverte de neutrinos de haute énergie d’origine astrophysique. Ces particules presque dépourvues de masse et de charge traversent la matière sans presque interagir avec elle, ce qui les rend extrêmement difficiles à détecter.

Professeur à l’Université du Wisconsin–Madison, Francis Halzen a défendu dès les années 1980 l’idée d’utiliser la glace de l’Antarctique comme immense détecteur. Cette vision a conduit à la création d’IceCube, installé près du pôle Sud et constitué de milliers de capteurs lumineux enfouis dans environ un kilomètre cube de glace.

En 2013, IceCube a identifié pour la première fois un flux de neutrinos de haute énergie provenant de l’extérieur du système solaire. Contrairement aux rayons cosmiques chargés, les neutrinos voyagent presque en ligne droite depuis leur source. Ils permettent ainsi aux scientifiques de remonter jusqu’aux phénomènes cosmiques extrêmes qui les produisent et d’étudier notamment l’environnement des trous noirs et des galaxies actives.

L’observatoire, financé notamment par la National Science Foundation (NSF), est piloté par une collaboration internationale coordonnée depuis l’Université du Wisconsin–Madison. Elle réunit environ 450 scientifiques issus de 58 institutions dans 14 pays. Avec les futures extensions d’IceCube, cette nouvelle forme d’astronomie devrait permettre d’explorer encore davantage les phénomènes les plus énergétiques de l’Univers.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/nobel-de-physique-2026-francis-halzen-recompense-pour-avoir-ouvert-une-nouvelle-fenetre-sur-lunivers/
Cover image: Christopher Michel / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

articles.headline: China’s Golden Week travellers go further but keep an eye on value
articles.dek: A 13-day break sends Chinese holidaymakers further afield, but spending stays careful.
articles.summary: A calendar quirk let Chinese workers stretch Golden Week to 13 days, and bookings rose, but travellers still favoured mid-range hotels, so brands must prove value to win their spending.

cover.alt: Crowds of travellers in a busy Chinese railway station hall
cover.credit: Photo: Joshua Fernandez / Unsplash, via DAO Insights

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Longer holiday itineraries reflect this year’s calendar, with three days of annual leave allowing a 13-day break
• Strong travel bookings coexist with selective spending: mid-range accommodation remains more popular than luxury hotels among surveyed travellers
• Brands have more opportunities to reach holidaymakers, but must demonstrate value to convert visitor traffic into purchases.

Chinese travellers are stretching their Golden Week itineraries to make the most of time off. That might sound like exactly the thing the tourism industry needs in China with spending still not picking up, but these longer holidays don’t look like they’ll supply the desired spending boom. Pre-holiday bookings show continued attention to value.

This year’s calendar helps explain the appetite. Taking three days of annual leave between Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day creates a 13-day break. That gives holidaymakers more time to head out on trips.

Trip.com reported that bookings for hotel stays of at least seven nights rose 123% against last Golden Week. Multi-destination itineraries also increased 84%, with average outbound trips exceeding nine days.

blocks.alt: Golden Week travel
blocks.caption: Image: Unsplash/Hassaan Malik

blocks.text: Yet consumer preference in accommodation shows spending caution. In Dragon Trail’s August survey, mid-range hotels were the most popular choice at 33%, while only 5% of respondents planned luxury stays: travelling for longer does not necessarily mean upgrading every part of the holiday.

The backdrop to this is an economy that’s been perpetually sluggish, and a holiday season that provides a good reason to spend. Authorities are working to encourage purchases. A nationwide cultural and tourism campaign running through October includes more than 20,000 planned events and over RMB310 million (about US $46.24 million) in consumer vouchers and subsidies.
The Dao view: Should Golden Week have been travel deal time?

If you’re a brand looking to snap up some holiday spending bucks, the opportunity lies in understanding which parts of a holiday consumers consider worth paying for. Longer journeys create more occasions for dining, shopping and entertainment, but also more days across which budgets must stretch. Busy destinations offer access to customers. They don’t guarantee generous spending. Whether travellers buy will depend on the value each offer delivers. Holiday promotions, anyone?
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/news/golden-week-travel/

articles.headline: Ancient Asian Carpet Making Is Finding New Life Through Modern Brands
articles.dek: An ancient craft dating back to the Han dynasty is being reworked by contemporary design brands.
articles.summary: Chinese carpet weaving, refined from the Han and Tang dynasties into Beijing, Ningxia and Tibetan styles, is being revived by modern brands that rework old patterns and techniques.

cover.alt: A person lying on a richly patterned blue and white rug wrapped in a striped blanket

blocks.text: In ancient China, carpets became prized objects among the wealthy, particularly during the Tang Dynasty. The craft of carpet making in China, however, dates back even earlier, with wool pile carpets already appearing in archaeological finds from the Han period. By the Tang Dynasty, carpet weaving in the Central Plains had become relatively mature.

blocks.caption: Chinese rug in ancient patterns. Image via Carpet Wiki.

blocks.text: Over time, carpet making developed into distinct regional traditions, including those of Beijing, the Central Plains, Ningxia, and Tibet. Each developed its own techniques, materials, colors, and visual language. Tibetan carpets, in particular, became closely associated with religious imagery and distinctive craftsmanship. Today, Tibetan carpets are still described as one of the “three great carpets,” alongside those from Turkey and Persia.

What makes these traditions particularly distinctive is not only their appearance but also the techniques used to make them. Traditional Beijing carpets, for example, developed a distinctive visual language shaped by Chinese decorative traditions. Beijing Palace carpets, also known as Gongtan (宫毯), became particularly associated with imperial and courtly settings. Their production involves detailed pattern design, careful material selection, and a series of highly skilled finishing processes.

blocks.caption: Beijing carpets were traditionally made for imperial use, requiring finer materials and more refined craftsmanship. Photo via Xiaohongshu.

blocks.text: Tibetan carpet making uses a different approach. Rather than tying the yarn directly onto the warp, weavers traditionally loop the yarn around a horizontal rod. Once a row is completed, the rod is removed, and the loops are cut, creating the carpet’s pile. This rod-based technique gives Tibetan carpets a distinctive structure and texture, setting them apart from Persian and Turkish knotting traditions.

blocks.caption: Tibetan women, respectfully known as “Aja,” weaving traditional Tibetan carpets. Picture via Pinterest.

blocks.text: Ningxia developed another important carpet tradition. Its carpets were historically used in Buddhist monasteries and were also associated with imperial production. Ningxia was an important source of pillar carpets for Tibetan and other Buddhist monasteries, showing how different regional carpet traditions were connected through trade, religion, and craft.

blocks.caption: Qing Dynasty Ningxia carpet with a “pixel art” style antique motif. Photo via Xiaohongshu.

blocks.text: Despite their long histories, many traditional carpet-making practices have faced pressure from industrial production and changing consumer habits. Now, contemporary brands are helping bring these traditions back into the conversation. Rather than treating traditional carpets solely as historical objects, brands such as Khawachen and SHARDAA Studios are introducing Tibetan carpet culture to a younger generation through contemporary products and design.

blocks.src: https://radii.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/喀瓦坚藏毯厂的夏日治愈之旅✨_9_Khawachen-喀瓦坚_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Khawachen owns a Tibetan rug factory and regularly shares the daily weaving process on social media, bringing traditional rug making to younger audiences around the world. Photo via Xiaohongshu.

blocks.text: For a new generation of consumers, the appeal of these carpets is no longer limited to their historical value. Their handmade construction, distinctive motifs, and regional identities offer another way to understand traditional craft through contemporary design. The revival of Chinese carpet making, therefore, is not simply about preserving an old craft. It is also about finding new contexts in which these regional traditions can remain relevant.

blocks.caption: Chinese tennis star Li Na filming an advertisement at the Khawachen Tibetan carpet factory. Photo via Songmont.

blocks.text: Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/classic-chinese-carpet-making-in-modern-brands

articles.headline: Post-Luxury Status Symbol #4: Hyper-Niche Expertise
articles.dek: Why the coolest person you know right now has a strangely specific hobby
articles.summary: As AI flattens taste into borrowed opinions, Eugene Healey says real status lies in obsessive niche expertise, and that brands should fund obsessives like patrons, not exploit them.

cover.alt: Close-up of a fishing fly being tied in a vice
cover.credit: Photo: Mike Cline / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

blocks.text: Every one of us is like a man who sees things in a dream and thinks that he knows them perfectly and then wakes up to find that he knows nothing. - Plato, Statesman

I’m not an AI-luddite, nor am I nostalgic for the world that preceded it. But it does increasingly feel that ChatGPT killed the last thing Google left alive from the decentralised web era: genuine curiosity.

Why develop a perspective when you can prompt one? Why spend years cultivating taste when you can ask an LLM to synthesise it for you in seconds? Everyone’s becoming a shallow generalist because the infrastructure now exists to fake depth without ever achieving it.
Soon enough, we’ll be living in a world of oceans an inch deep, everyone paddling around in puddles of borrowed expertise, vomiting up aggregated opinions they’ve mistaken for knowledge.

In this landscape, real status comes from the inverse: hyper-niche expertise. Not the performed kind that fits neatly into content formats, but the obsessive, decades-long devotion to something so specific that your knowledge becomes idiosyncratic, incongruous and contradictory - making it irreproducible by any algorithm.
The Cult of One Thing

It’s not what you possess, it’s the depth with which you devote yourself to something that transcends all the metrics and the ultra-productivity of the 21st century. Having hyper-niche expertise is a way of resisting the “harmonisation of tastes,” as Igor Schwarzmann tells Chayka in his book Filterworld - the algorithmic flattening that makes everything look and feel the same.

This harmonisation isn’t confined to algorithms, it’s metastasised into physical space. As someone who travels internationally often for work, it is always strange to experience this frictionless interchangeability, I can wake up disoriented in Lisbon or Berlin after 24 hours of flying and feel immediately, depressingly oriented. Aesop hand soap seems to follow me around the world (derogatory).
The status now comes from resisting this sameness through deep, idiosyncratic commitment to something the algorithm would never surface.

This is why Tokyo remains the best shopping city in the world. Every other major capital has its own IRL version of AI slop: the same international flagships, merchandised identically, pushing the same collections. Tokyo gives you access to hyper-specific perspectives - stores curated by individuals with decades of obsessive devotion to one thing that only a post-growth economy could cultivate. A Jura-only wine bar, a store where everything is derived from the same shade of indigo blue, a bookshop that only stocks philosophy from the 1960s.
Brands as Patrons (or Parasites)
I have said before that the vast majority of brands do not ‘create’ culture - they are simply not influential enough in shaping societal norms, values, or opinions.

Instead, ‘culture’ brands are those who are effective at facilitating exchange between cultural and economic capital: identifying complementary individuals or movements, giving them platforms to express themselves, and paying people fairly for their time and effort.
Now that the algorithm has flattened everything, there is nothing more culturally dull for a brand than a predictable big name, mass reach collab.

Instead, ‘culture’ brands must act like eccentric wealthy patrons - championing the obsessives no algorithm would ever surface, funding the projects no KPI would justify, and appearing interesting by virtue of the strange and obscure company they keep.

This is partly why Gucci partnered with Francis Bourgeois in 2022. There was something magnetic about the purity of his train obsession - a completely unironic devotion that felt like an antidote to the cynical irony that dominates online culture. This was a perfect example of product-culture fit.

Other examples provide a warning. Nicheness comes with its own risks precisely because audience relationships are indexed so high on meaning - perhaps even more so for Creators than brands themselves.

The Kindle ad with Jack Edwards tanked whatever credibility this previously trusted BookToker had. Here we had someone who’d spent years building authority by preaching the opposite of what Amazon represents - supporting independent bookstores, championing physical books, cultivating literary taste beyond bestseller algorithms. The poor guy ended up wiping his entire social media presence.

So many brands still treat Creators like sock puppets: using their name, image, and likeness, while stuffing their endlessly focus grouped, reach-as-many-as-possible-while-offending-the-least tone of voice down their throat.

To this I often have to say to them: what the fuck do you think you’re paying for? Do you, corporate marketing manager with 15 years of back-to-back FMCG experience, have intimate knowledge of the mushroom foraging community you’re so desperately trying to sell into?
You are paying for SPECIFICITY. Let the Creator be specific.
What Brands Can Actually Do
If you’re building for this shift, the question is how to enable obsession without destroying it.

Your brand needs to learn to act like an editor. Bring together niche creators and pay them to make things without forcing your logo into every frame. Let your brand become the canvas - where the brand associations are built as an aggregate mosaic of who you choose to associate yourself with.
The opportunity is more than content, it’s in the cultural capital that transfers to your brand when you’re seen as someone who funds things that don’t need to exist but should exist anyway.

This is the Red Bull model: fund extreme athletes, underground music scenes, niche sports that would never get mainstream sponsorship, then absorb the cultural credibility as ownable brand associations with energy, passion, and of course, risk.

This demands patience and a willingness to fund work without obvious KPIs, an enduring challenge in brand where, arguably, we are one of the only disciplines in the business that has to think beyond quarterly shareholder meetings. But the alternative is contributing to the everything-everywhere-sameness that’s already drowning your category.
Remember that half of the job of brand is being remembered, and the other half is being remembered for the right thing. So perhaps, try doing something memorable?

Not being everything, everywhere, all at once is actually human. That’s the real contradiction we’re living in: trying to embrace the infinite everything the algorithm throws at us while inhabiting a finite body and a finite life, with a beginning and an end.

Plato was right: we think we know things perfectly until we wake up and realise we know nothing. But at least now we know a lot about very little. And in a world of shallow puddles, that might be enough.
Source: Eugene Healey — https://eugenehealey.substack.com/p/hyper-niche-expertise

articles.headline: Une bactérie de grenouille montre un puissant effet anticancéreux chez la souris
articles.dek: News · 7 octobre 2026
articles.summary: Une bactérie de l’intestin d’une rainette japonaise, Ewingella americana, a fait disparaître des tumeurs colorectales chez la souris en les attaquant et en stimulant l’immunité.

cover.alt: Image au microscope de cellules cancéreuses roses aux contours irréguliers
cover.credit: Photo: National Cancer Institute / Unsplash, via Republic of Innovation

blocks.text: Une bactérie naturellement présente dans l’intestin d’une grenouille japonaise pourrait ouvrir une nouvelle piste dans la lutte contre le cancer. Des chercheurs du Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (JAIST) ont identifié Ewingella americana, une bactérie capable de provoquer une régression complète de tumeurs dans un modèle murin de cancer colorectal.

L’équipe a étudié des bactéries provenant du microbiote intestinal de deux amphibiens, Dryophytes japonicus et Cynops pyrrhogaster, ainsi que du lézard Takydromus tachydromoides. Parmi les souches testées, E. americana, isolée chez la rainette japonaise, s’est distinguée par une forte activité antitumorale.

Son action repose sur deux mécanismes complémentaires. La bactérie s’accumule préférentiellement dans les tissus tumoraux, où elle exerce un effet toxique direct sur les cellules cancéreuses. Elle stimule également la réponse immunitaire en mobilisant notamment les lymphocytes T et B ainsi que les neutrophiles.

Dans les expériences réalisées sur des souris, une seule administration intraveineuse a entraîné une régression complète des tumeurs dans le modèle étudié et s’est révélée plus efficace que les traitements de comparaison, dont la doxorubicine et un anticorps anti-PD-L1. Aucun effet indésirable majeur n’a été observé aux doses testées.
Publiés dans la revue Gut Microbes, ces résultats restent précliniques et devront être confirmés par d’autres études avant toute application chez l’être humain.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/une-bacterie-de-grenouille-montre-un-puissant-effet-anticancereux-chez-la-souris/

articles.headline: The mooncake pop-up highlighting Walmart’s own-brand ingredients
articles.dek: Walmart blew up a mooncake gift box into a Shenzhen pop-up to introduce its young private label.
articles.summary: Walmart turned a giant mooncake gift box into an eight-day Shenzhen pop-up for its Woji Fresh private label, using tastings and apothecary displays to sell the idea of simple ingredients.

cover.alt: A wooden mooncake-box pop-up pavilion with shoppers in a Shenzhen plaza

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Walmart turned a mooncake gift box into an interactive Shenzhen pop-up, using seasonal interest to introduce shoppers to Woji Fresh
• Apothecary displays, ingredient origins and tastings made the private label’s emphasis on simple ingredients tangible
• The campaign connected Mid-Autumn gifting with Woji Fresh’s wider move into traditional Chinese dietary wellness, helping build an identity beyond Walmart

Mooncake business can be fierce. Grabbing consumer attention for the Mid-Autumn Festival can take up big parts of a supermarket’s ad budget and shelf space at this time of year. For many brands, packaging plays as much of a part as what’s inside the box.
Walmart (沃尔玛) has played on this relationship in a Shenzhen pop-up where it enlarged a mooncake box to 10,000 x scale and used it a location to push a message for its private-label Woji Fresh (沃集鲜).

Launched in November 2025, the label’s philosophy is simple ingredients, sourced well and sold fresh. The eight-day activation turned a seasonal product into an introduction to the young private label, and a way to hold its own in a crowded market. It did it all while tying the message to some deeply traditional Chinese messaging at a time when it hits hardest. The results hit No. 2 on Douyin’s trending list.
Gift box blow up

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/今年中秋，我们开了家简单食铺_1_沃尔玛_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Walmart mooncake pop-up
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/沃尔玛

blocks.text: The pop-up’s centrepiece was a baizigui – a compartmentalised cabinet found at traditional Chinese medicine shops. Illuminated drawers displayed ginseng, lily bulbs, dried tangerine peel and goji berries. Ingredients were presented through a familiar cultural setting.

Visitors could pull open drawers labelled with auspicious phrases to discover blessing cards. These could be exchanged for mooncakes, connecting the installation directly to a product trial. Flavours included apple and astragalus, alongside a low-sugar combination of chestnut, osmanthus and Tieguanyin tea.

It was a direct link to the medicinal links between Chinese medicine and food. That was itself a way to push Woji’s ingredient-first messaging and the heritage brand they partnered with for this year’s mooncake range.
Deep roots

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/今年中秋，我们开了家简单食铺_7_沃尔玛_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Walmart mooncake pop-up
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/沃尔玛

blocks.text: For the mooncake range, Woji Fresh partnered with century-old traditional Chinese medicine business Li Liang Ji (李良济). There is a wider commercial connection. In July, Woji announced a food-and-medicine-themed range that spans drinks, bakery, snacks and dairy, with more than 100 products planned.

That means its mooncake event is a seasonal introduction to an existing direction in product development. Walmart’s Mid-Autumn range was available through its stores and app, though Shenzhen made a solid choice of setting for the delivery of this message.

Shenzhen’s province of Guangdong has long associations with herbal teas and soups that make the overlap between food and traditional dietary wellness familiar. The installation was simply adapting that everyday culture into a photogenic retail experience.
The Dao view: Giving a private label something to stand for

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/今年中秋，我们开了家简单食铺_8_沃尔玛_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/沃尔玛

blocks.text: Woji Fresh needs shoppers to understand why they might actively choose their products. The campaign’s strongest move was to build the experience around the product itself. Product here worked as both display and reward for interaction. In both cases, the brand story was reinforced.

That coherence can help Woji Fresh build recognition independently of Walmart – also useful. Chinese shoppers will be familiar with Walmart, but Woji needs to stand out as something consumers will seek out of trust.

Apothecary imagery and traditional formulations are there to communicate a reason why that trust is well placed. Mid-Autumn Festival made an apt time for that message to circulate. The resulting pop-up did everything an offline activation should: further a brand message, do it in a way that engages visitors, and strike up engagement online.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/works/walmart-mooncake-pop-up/

articles.headline: Post-Luxury status symbols #5: Creating Community
articles.dek: Why the 'Host' has become the ultimate aspirational identity
articles.summary: With third places vanishing, Eugene Healey argues the host who can build real community has become an aspirational identity, one that takes space, energy and money.

cover.alt: Three friends laughing and raising their glasses at a restaurant dinner

blocks.text: There is a certain mysticism - or morbid fascination - in re-watching old Friends or Sex and the City episodes, where, somehow, we come to see as almost idyllic the act of gathering around an object, be it a Cosmo, or just a languid coffee and chat with our friends. Has creating memorable moments become one of the last luxuries most craved by our society? If so, those who create, curate, and moderate these spaces emerge as the true holders of status.
The Death of Third Places

We live in a world where socialisation seems to be hanging by a thread - observe the fucking dire statistic that Only 4.1 percent of Americans attended or hosted a social event on an average weekend or holiday in 2023.

Much of this can be put down to the disappearance of third places. What we are facing is the fact that these places for leisure and human connection - which, by the way, are defined by democratic accessibility - require infrastructure that no longer exists or has been systematically dismantled.

Privatisation of public space. Hostile architecture designed to prevent lingering. Coffee shops optimised for turnover. Libraries defunded. Parks surveilled. The logic of capital doesn’t accommodate spaces where people gather without transacting, ergo they get squeezed out of existence.

When third places vanish - and when governments and institutions, both public and private, fail to guarantee spaces for leisure and human nurturing with others - we’re forced to create these spaces themselves. However, for logistical, monetary, infrastructural reasons, and more, the spaces that we, or a particular group of people, are able to create are rarely designed for everyone.
On Reanimation in Zombie Times

What is increasingly emerging as an ‘evolution’ of third places is not really the third place at all - it’s a dolled up reanimated corpse typical of the Zombie times we live in. Curated, exclusive, filtered, branded.

Private fashion salons for friends of the house, itinerant chef’s tables, invitation-only screenings. All operate within the same logic: access itself as the currency. These are not events designed for mass participation; rather carefully curated moments where presence signals belonging, where being invited matters more than being seen.

Nobody is immune. The ultra-rich are trading traditional luxury assets for luxury experiences. Even for them, authentic experience has been replaced by its performance. It’s no longer enough to attend an event; you must be part of the show - and for many, being part of the show now means creating moments within pop culture. Wimbledon has surged in recent years, in great part due to the fact that it places the social theatre of the event on the same pedestal as the sport itself.
To be Known, not just Seen
A gap has emerged between the aspiration once shaped by the promises of early social media and what this shift reveals instead: our desire to be known, not just seen.

Being seen is algorithmic - 10,000 followers watching your stories. Being known is analog - eight people around a table who remember how you take your coffee. The first scales infinitely. The second doesn’t scale at all. And that’s precisely what makes it luxury.

Being known requires time, repetition, and crucially, vulnerability. It means showing up in the same room with the same people often enough that patterns emerge. Known people remember your coffee order. They know which topics make you light up and which ones you’d rather avoid. They can tell when something’s wrong before you say it.
The Host as Aspirational Identity
If everyone is selling access to an inner circle, what constitutes real community? The answer lies in the hosts.

Creating genuine community has become a powerful status symbol because it requires a specific and increasingly rare set of skills. The host must have enough cultural capital and sensitivity to read the habitus of each guest and anticipate frictions; who speaks to whom and when. What kind of activities, games, and conversations are right for that environment. And they know how to build an atmosphere that enables people to walk in, drop their guard, and authentically connect.

This is an exercise in precision not unlike Anna Wintour’s Met Gala seating chart: the art of creating human connection without the attendees realising the work involved. The effortlessness is the performance, is the status symbol.

The success of books such as The Art of Gathering or games like We’re Not Really Strangers speak directly to this: they’re products for the architects of these spaces, who become behavioural designers. The manual exists because the skill is no longer ambient. We’ve forgotten how to gather, so we need instructions.
Grounding this for a second in material reality: hosting requires resources most people simply don’t have.

You need space large enough to accommodate guests comfortably. In an era of shrinking apartments and rising rents, this alone is prohibitive for many. You need disposable income for food, drinks, and the inevitable wear and tear on your home. You need time - not just the hours of the gathering itself, but the preparation before and cleanup after.

You need energy. In my piece on wasteful time, I identified how post-optimisation is only accessible to those with surplus capacity. The same applies here. After a 50-hour work week, after side hustles and algorithmic content creation and emotional labor, who has the reserves to host? To perform ease and abundance even when you’re exhausted?

You need geographic proximity to a friend group. Precarity scatters people - jobs in different cities, cheaper rent further out as the inner city YoPro becomes the outer city parent, the constant churn of relocation. Building the kind of recurring community that makes hosting worthwhile requires stability most people don’t have.

This ability to create community is as much about surplus as skill. This is why the Instagram chefs, the salon hosts, the dinner party architects, are often those with significant class privilege, even if they perform bohemian aesthetics.
Creating Brands Outside the Panopticon

The easy answer here is to tell brands to stay the fuck away from ‘community building’. More difficult is to admit that they may have a role in rebuilding community infrastructure - IF they can play by the rules.

This connects to everything from the previous installments of this series: How can you create warm, private, safe atmospheres where the people present care about the thing, not being seen at the thing? How can you create post-optimisation spaces where your activation isn’t just about trying to get people to post about it - it’s enough for them to just exist and spend time there?
The paradox here is that brands need scale, while community requires intimacy. The solution is what we might call anti-spectacle: spaces where presence matters more than performance.
Not because phones are bad, but because the possibility of documentation changes behaviour. Remove that possibility, and people can actually be present.

BeReal attempted to solve this through tech - randomized photo prompts to capture ‘authentic’ moments. But tech solutions to social problems inevitably become more problems. Alarms to take the photo. Anxiety about streaks. The mechanics diluted the purpose.

Real anti-spectacle can’t be coded. It requires human curation. Renaissance Fairs and Comic Cons understand this instinctively: create space for people to obsess together without performing for an external audience, and community emerges organically. No one’s performing cool. Everyone’s geeking out.

How can you create offline experiences built around hyper-specific niches that give a group of people the chance to really nerd out over something? Forget ‘wellness’, give me Victorian taxidermy. Not “gaming,” but a speedrunning of Croc: Legend of the Gobbos. The narrower the focus, the deeper the connection.
Because if your “community” can be switched off with the press of a button, you don’t have a community. You have customers.
Source: Eugene Healey — https://eugenehealey.substack.com/p/creating-community
Cover image: PattayaPatrol / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

articles.headline: FiberMotor : un moteur aussi fin qu’un fil pour la robotique portable
articles.dek: News · 7 octobre 2026
articles.summary: L’EPFL a créé FiberMotor, un moteur souple de 1 à 3 mm fait de deux fibres coulissantes, qui pourrait animer des exosquelettes, des prothèses légères et des vêtements haptiques.

cover.alt: Un dispositif robotique d’assistance à la marche porté sur les jambes

blocks.text: Des scientifiques de l’École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) ont développé FiberMotor, un moteur flexible de seulement 1 à 3 millimètres de diamètre capable de convertir directement l’énergie électrique en mouvement linéaire. Cette innovation pourrait faciliter le développement d’exosquelettes souples, de prothèses légères ou encore de dispositifs haptiques intégrés aux vêtements.

Conçu au Laboratoire des microsystèmes souples (LMTS) de la Faculté des sciences et techniques de l’ingénieur de l’EPFL, le dispositif est constitué de deux fibres creuses concentriques entourées d’électrodes hélicoïdales. Lorsqu’une tension électrique est appliquée, les forces électrostatiques provoquent le glissement d’une fibre dans l’autre, produisant un mouvement bidirectionnel comparable à celui de tubes télescopiques.

Contrairement à de nombreux muscles artificiels, dont l’amplitude est limitée par la déformation des matériaux, la course du FiberMotor dépend essentiellement de la longueur des fibres. Sa conception sans engrenages lui permet également de céder lorsqu’une force opposée est appliquée, une propriété intéressante pour des interactions plus naturelles et sûres entre humains et machines.

Lors des essais, un moteur a pu supporter une charge statique d’environ 75 grammes, tandis que quatre FiberMotors regroupés ont permis de soulever une barre de 46 grammes et d’actionner un doigt robotique. Les chercheurs ont également intégré le système dans un prototype de vêtement au niveau du genou.
Les travaux de Sylvain Schaller et Herbert Shea ont été publiés dans Advanced Materials. La recherche a bénéficié du soutien du Fonds national suisse et de la Novo Nordisk Foundation.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/fibermotor-un-moteur-aussi-fin-quun-fil-pour-la-robotique-portable/
Cover image: Morio / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

articles.headline: Peet’s X Helly Hansen: The cat gets another outdoor partnership
articles.dek: After Salomon and The North Face, Peet’s sets sail with a new outdoor partner.
articles.summary: Peet’s Coffee teams up with Helly Hansen on sailing-themed drinks, merchandise and mini-program rewards, its third outdoor tie-in after Salomon and The North Face.

cover.alt: A white sail with the Helly Hansen and Peet’s logos on a blue sea

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Peet’s × Helly Hansen extends the existing Great Voyager coffee range into sailing-themed drinks, merchandise and mini-program rewards
• Following Salomon and The North Face, the partnership builds a consistent association between flavour discovery and outdoor adventure
• Outdoor partnerships could help Peet’s compete on lifestyle appeal in a coffee market where that message stands out

Peet’s Coffee (皮爷咖啡) has partnered with Helly Hansen on an outdoor-themed collaboration. It brings sailing imagery to limited-edition drinks, merchandise and mini-program activities. The link-up’s starting point is already on Pete’s coffee menu: the Great Voyager coffee-bean range.

Two items work the maritime theme into something drinkable. Deep Blue Ice Sea cold brew – a drink that combines nutty coffee flavours with a blue milk-foam topping. Azure Sea Breeze then steps in with a mix of coconut water with high-protein milk and coffee, finished with light-blue foam.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/官宣！大航海家-共赴风味新境_1_Peets皮爷咖啡_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Peet’s Helly Hansen
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/Peet’s皮爷咖啡

blocks.text: Fridge magnets, floor mats and insulated cups carry the collaboration out of the store. Customers can also illuminate what are being called flavour landmarks through purchases in Peet’s mini-program and enter draws for collaboration gift boxes. These include a sailing-themed grand prize (No word on what that actually is yet).
The partnership follows a recognisable route for Peet’s. In December 2025, its Salomon collaboration paired winter drinks with outdoorsy coffee experiences at Songhua Lake ski resort.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/📢航海周边上线｜把蔚蓝深海带回家⛵️_1_Peets皮爷咖啡_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Peet’s Helly Hansen
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/Peet’s皮爷咖啡

blocks.text: In May 2026, The North Face partnership accompanied the launch of Peet’s Yunnan Menglian single-origin coffee. That campaign connected mountain landscapes with flavour exploration and extended into selected North Face stores. With that in mind, Helly Hansen makes a good fit for that theme of exploration and the big outdoors.
The Dao view: A different collaboration angle

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/联名上新｜四条风味航线，等你来探索👊_1_Peets皮爷咖啡_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/Peet’s皮爷咖啡

blocks.text: Repeated outdoor partnerships are there to help Peet’s build a consistent lifestyle around flavour discovery. The existing Great Voyager name gives the discovery theme a product to connect to.

Skiing, mountains and now sailing turn the abstract idea of discovering coffee into recognisable pursuits. Repeating the outdoor theme across different partners could help these campaigns build on one another, giving customers a clearer sense of what Peet’s stands for beyond each limited-edition launch.

articles.headline: Post-Luxury status symbols #6: Quality Sleep
articles.dek: Status comes for the unconscious world, and final thoughts on the series
articles.summary: In the series finale, Eugene Healey argues eight hours of untracked sleep is the new status symbol, as trackers and sleep products turn rest into one more thing to optimise.

cover.alt: A neatly made bed with plush white pillows in a bright bedroom

blocks.text: “After thirty years together, sleeping is the new having sex. “That was amazing, wasn’t it!” one or the other of us will say upon waking in the morning. How did we become these people? I wonder. — David Sedaris, Pearls”
Welcome to the finale of the post-luxury status symbols series.
The ability to consistently get 8 hours of great sleep has become a status symbol. Yes, really.

What makes this one even more tiresome than the rest is that it’s not just something being performed - it’s being gamified. We’ve quantified the last refuge from productivity. The last refuge from productivity, literal unconsciousness, is now another metric to optimise. How did we get here?
The Great Inversion

For decades, sleeping little was the status symbol, the inevitable consequence of a society in which being busy equates to being desired. For some, it still is: Japanese PM Takaichi claims she only needs two hours a night. Thatcher famously needed four; it seems shrinkflation has hit us everywhere.
But something seems to have shifted. Now the flex is the opposite: getting your full eight hours, being consistently well-rested.
What changed?

Well, arguably we’ve collectively burned out. The grind economy promised that if we just optimised harder through 5am wake-ups, biohacking, side hustles, we’d achieve the prosperity our parents stumbled into. Instead, we’re more exhausted than ever. In that context, demonstrating you’re not exhausted becomes the ultimate flex.
But, if you’ve observed one through line with this series - once a behaviour becomes aspirational, it becomes ripe for optimisation.
The Sleep Capture Game

The philosopher C. Thi Nguyen has created much thoughtful work around the dangers of gamification. When we quantify anything, we run the risk of losing interest in the underlying value in favour of the metric. The game captures our values by offering us a simpler, more measurable target.
Fitbit originally mastered this impulse - health took a backseat to hitting 10k steps. The number became the goal.
And so too now, do we find this in the field of sleep tracking.

Oura Rings or Eight Sleep mattresses promise to optimise your rest by tracking your REM cycles, deep sleep percentages, heart rate variability, body temperature fluctuations. They capture you immediately through real data and actionable insights.
You wake up and check your ring. 82 sleep score. Not great. Deep sleep was only 18%. You feel fine, but the device says you’re not recovering properly.

It’s a natural escalation here into further spending: cooler room, magnesium supplements, mouth tape to ensure nasal breathing (the sleep aids market is predicted to hit up to USD 160 billion by 2034).

This is the ultimate irony of the sleep optimisation industry: in trying to improve rest, it’s made rest impossible. Once again, quantification has corrupted the underlying value, and we find another domain in which the individual must perform for their digital god.
The Sleep Hierarchy
In fact, from this we can map a clear hierarchy of sleep privilege:
1: Sleep Poverty Working multiple jobs. Noisy housing. No control over schedule. Caregiving responsibilities that fragment sleep. Economic precarity that makes rest impossible. This is the majority.
2. Sleep Maintenance Average people trying to get by with basic sleep hygiene. A regular-ish bedtime, eye masks, white noise machines.

3. Sleep Optimisation Tracking devices. Expensive mattresses. Climate-controlled bedrooms. Supplements. Sleep coaches. Blue-light-blocking glasses. The full apparatus of the wellness industry deployed to perfect rest.

4. Sleep Luxury Being so secure you don’t need to optimise at all. Sleeping without tracking. Waking without alarms. Never checking your sleep score because your life is structured such that rest happens naturally.

What emerges is the same trend across all post-luxury status symbols: modern society stripping away what used to be natural phenomena, brands rush in to sell solutions - often worsening the problem by creating entirely new anxieties around optimisation. Finally, status is formed through the ability to go post-optimisation.
Monetising Unconsciousness
There are many examples of the perverse manners in which sleep is monetised across our society.

IKEA’s Sleepfluencers campaign gave away blackout blinds if bedrooms functioned as free advertising for their products. It won awards at major festivals. But what they gained was advertising space inside your most private window. How much can the desire to be in the dark, in your room, be monetised?

This logic is reinforced by the normalisation of influencers like Jacky Boehm, who emerged during the boom of streamers monetising sleep, encouraging audiences to send gifts to wake him up. Sleep-as-content, productive unconsciousness.

Baudrillard considered the body to be capitalism’s last great object - for once it is optimised, aestheticised, and managed, nothing remains outside the system. This is where we seem to find ourselves, even in our sleep - generating data, hosting advertisements, producing value.
The great irony here is that in reclaiming sleep as a status symbol, a form of resistance to grind culture, we have simply created a new game to flail around in, a new way to fail at being human.
We can’t gamify our way to genuine rest. We can’t optimise our way to unconsciousness. Yet structural conditions make untracked, unpressured sleep inaccessible to most people.

The single mother working multiple jobs doesn’t need an Oura Ring. She needs affordable housing, a living wage, employers who respect that humans require rest. Sleep should be considered a fundamental right, not a personal responsibility. But that would require admitting the problem is structural, not individual. Structural problems, of course, require collective solutions that threaten the very hierarchies that status depends upon.
Final notes on the post-luxury series

If you’ve inferred a slightly dystopian tone through this series, you would be correct. But I suspect the reason these pieces have performed so well is because they speak to a shame we all feel but struggle to articulate: we’re trapped in a game we can’t afford to stop playing.

I know my audience. I’ve met many of you, real or online, and one common trait runs through: you’re thoughtful, and you’re conflicted. We desire the world to be better, and yet we are deeply interested in notions of status, or success, and how it can be accrued.

Once, this may have been vanity. Now, it’s survival instinct in an economy where status directly correlates with security. When basic needs like rest, privacy, time, and community become luxuries, understanding how status operates becomes a matter of strategy.
At the end of the day, there is no app or amount of money that can truly help us cut ourselves some slack. The only way to genuinely rest would be to stop tracking, stop optimising, stop performing.

But perhaps this acute awareness of being caught in a Chinese finger trap is itself the first step toward something different. The post-luxury status symbols I’ve outlined across this series - connected privacy, wasteful time, having children, niche expertise, creating community, quality sleep - all point to the same underlying desire: to reclaim what has been stolen and repackaged as luxury. The basics of human existence.

What gives me hope (alongside meeting all of you) is that we’re getting better at seeing the game for what it is. There is increasingly a collective literacy around how status operates, how gamification corrupts values, how optimisation and performativity become their own traps.

The work ahead is collective. It’s organising for structural change: housing as a right, living wages, work-life boundaries enforced by law not personal discipline, sleep protected as essential to human dignity.

And in the meantime, we can be honest about the game we’re in. We can help each other navigate it without pretending it’s natural or inevitable. We can name the contradictions and live in them consciously rather than being consumed by them unknowingly.
That’s not a solution. But it’s better than a fucking Oura ring.
Source: Eugene Healey — https://eugenehealey.substack.com/p/quality-sleep

articles.headline: Un blazar record observé à huit milliards d’années-lumière
articles.dek: News · 7 octobre 2026
articles.summary: Avec le télescope LST-1 et MAGIC à La Palma, une équipe incluant l’UNIGE a capté le blazar OP 313, le plus lointain jamais vu à très haute énergie, à huit milliards d’années-lumière.

cover.alt: Le grand télescope Tcherenkov LST-1 sous un ciel étoilé

blocks.text: Une équipe internationale comprenant des scientifiques de l’Université de Genève (UNIGE) a détecté le blazar le plus lointain jamais observé à très haute énergie. Baptisé OP 313, cet objet situé à environ huit milliards d’années-lumière offre une occasion exceptionnelle d’étudier l’Univers lointain et les phénomènes extrêmes qui entourent les trous noirs supermassifs.

Les blazars sont des noyaux actifs de galaxies alimentés par un trou noir supermassif. Ils émettent de puissants jets de matière et de rayonnement dont l’un est orienté presque directement vers la Terre. OP 313 a été détecté grâce au prototype Large-Sized Telescope LST-1 du Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) et aux télescopes MAGIC, installés à l’Observatoire du Roque de los Muchachos, sur l’île de La Palma, en Espagne.

Les observations ont révélé des rayons gamma de très haute énergie provenant de cette source, située à un décalage vers le rouge de 0,997. Leur analyse permet aux scientifiques d’étudier le fond diffus extragalactique, constitué de la lumière accumulée au cours de l’histoire cosmique, mais aussi de mieux comprendre l’accélération des particules dans les jets produits autour des trous noirs.

L’UNIGE joue un rôle important dans le projet puisque l’Université dirige le consortium suisse du CTAO. La collaboration CTAO LST rassemble par ailleurs plus de 500 scientifiques et ingénieurs issus de 25 institutions dans 11 pays. Cette découverte illustre les performances du LST-1 avant l’entrée en service complète du réseau de télescopes LST.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/un-blazar-record-observe-a-huit-milliards-dannees-lumiere/

articles.headline: Out of Focus: Rednote probes at reality with nine creator-led short films
articles.dek: Rednote paired nine of its community filmmakers with actors to explore AI and identity.
articles.summary: Rednote commissioned nine creator-led short films on reality, identity and AI, with advice from FIRST and a cinema screening, in a bid to keep distinctive creators on the platform.

cover.alt: A film poster showing a dinner table scene under green Chinese title lettering

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Rednote paired nine community creators with actors to explore reality, identity and AI through short films
• FIRST’s advisory support and cinema screening gave emerging filmmakers exposure beyond their usual platform audiences
• The project shows how opportunities for creators could strengthen Rednote’s community and attract distinctive content

When images can be fabricated and identities endlessly edited, what remains real? Rednote (小红书) has put that question to nine of its community of film makers. They have produced nine short films under the theme Out of Focus (失世界真中).

The films give anxieties about artificial reality a personal dimension. One called Make a Wish (许个愿吧) explores a mother–daughter relationship reshaped by AI. Evaporation (蒸发), looks into a world where a person can be copied, modified and sold.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/世界失真中，9部小红书超级作品正式官宣！_1_短电影薯_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: out of focus
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/短电影薯

blocks.text: FIRST Film was on hand to deliver advisory support throughout the projects. Actors were hired to star in the films too. And, as part of the campaign, these films made it to the big screen as part of a FIRST Film festival. The films have since begun appearing on the creators’ own Rednote accounts to keep creators’ channels central to distribution.

Ironically enough, the very force that makes us question so much of what we see these days – artificial intelligence – also helped produce some of the work. Director Shanyin said he used it to supplement drawings and photographic imagery in his film Four of Me Live in the Room (房间里住着四个我). Does that undermine the project’s entire aim, or add a new shade of complexity?
The Dao view: Making human expression a brand asset

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/世界失真中，9部小红书超级作品正式官宣！_4_短电影薯_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/短电影薯

blocks.text: Supporting distinctive content creators strengthens Rednote’s connection to the very community it helps promote. For a platform where recommendations gain value from the people behind them, that’s huge.

Pairing community filmmakers with established actors and putting their work on a cinema screen shows what Rednote can offer users beyond views and likes. If you’re an aspiring creator, access to collaborators and industry attention is a solid reason to keep publishing there.

In return, Rednote feeds get distinctive work that gives the platform’s audience a reason to keep logging on. It’s a neat feedback loop and Rednote know it. Check out their One Day in the World campaign for another example of how well this works.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/news/as-the-world-distorts-rednote/

articles.headline: Zhang Yimou Teases A Homegrown Chinese ‘Three-Body Problem’ Film
articles.dek: The director confirms at Busan that his own adaptation of Liu Cixin’s saga is well underway.
articles.summary: Zhang Yimou told the Busan film festival that his Three-Body Problem film is underway, with a script shaped by more than 400,000 fan comments gathered online.

cover.alt: A grid of dramatic character posters for a Three-Body Problem adaptation

blocks.text: Finished binging the Netflix adaptation of Liu Cixin’s mind-bending sci-fi saga, The Three-Body Problem? Sad that it’s all over? Well, Legendary Chinese auteur Zhang Yimou just dropped a massive teaser at the 31st Busan International Film Festival, confirming that his own homegrown cinematic adaptation is well underway. Good news for us all!

blocks.alt: RADII shares the film director Zhang Yimou's announcement at the 31st Busan International Film Festival that he's filming a film adaptation of Liu Cixin's 'Three-Body Problem, famous from its Netflix series.
blocks.caption: Legendary Chinese director Zhang Yimou at the 31st Busan International Film Festival. Image via SBS Star.

blocks.text: Speaking as the president of Busan’s main competition jury, Zhang revealed that he and his team have spent years meticulously polishing the script. Taking a decidedly modern, Gen Z-friendly approach to development, the director brought on a team to scour the internet and collect over 400,000 comments from die-hard fans. All of this done to deeply understand audience expectations and ensure the film honors the sprawling legacy of the original novels.

blocks.alt: RADII shares the film director Zhang Yimou's announcement at the 31st Busan International Film Festival that he's filming a film adaptation of Liu Cixin's 'Three-Body Problem, famous from its Netflix series.
blocks.caption: The original story of The Three-Body Problem, written by Cixin Liu. Image via Macmillan Publishers.

blocks.text: “The Three-Body Problem is a great work of science fiction, but it’s hard to photograph,” Zhang explained from the Busan Cinema Center stage. “I will sincerely study the hopes and demands of the audience and hopefully make a good movie.” This comes from a director known for his films being picturesque masterpieces at any pause.

blocks.alt: RADII shares the film director Zhang Yimou's announcement at the 31st Busan International Film Festival that he's filming a film adaptation of Liu Cixin's 'Three-Body Problem, famous from its Netflix series.
blocks.caption: The official character posters for Netflix’ 3 Body Problem. Image via Reddit.

blocks.text: For audiences only familiar with the recent Netflix series, Zhang’s involvement is big time for Chinese cinema. Arguably China’s most celebrated filmmaker, Zhang is renowned for weaving stunning visual palettes and grandly staged choreography in sweeping epics like Hero, House of Flying Daggers, and the iconic Raise the Red Lantern, to name a few.

This upcoming project promises a Chinese cultural lens on the extraterrestrial epic, distinctly separate from the English-language Netflix series spearheaded by the creators of Game of Thrones. With Zhang Yimou’s masterful eye for cinematic spectacle combined with Liu Cixin’s vast universe, this is shaping up to be, well… nobody’s problem at all.
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/zhang-yimou-chinese-three-body-problem-film-busan

articles.headline: Narcolepsie : une nouvelle hypothèse ouvre la voie à des traitements potentiellement réversibles
articles.dek: News · 7 octobre 2026
articles.summary: Des chercheurs de l’UNIL suggèrent que la narcolepsie de type 1 viendrait d’une mise sous silence épigénétique du gène de l’hypocrétine, ce qui la rendrait peut-être réversible.

cover.alt: Un homme endormi au volant de sa voiture garée

blocks.text: La narcolepsie de type 1 pourrait ne pas être provoquée uniquement par la destruction des neurones producteurs d’hypocrétine, comme le suppose l’hypothèse auto-immune dominante. Des chercheurs de l’Université de Lausanne (UNIL) avancent une autre piste: le déficit en hypocrétine, ou orexine, pourrait résulter d’une mise sous silence épigénétique du gène HCRT.

Cette maladie neurologique chronique se caractérise principalement par une somnolence diurne excessive et par la cataplexie, une perte soudaine du tonus musculaire déclenchée notamment par des émotions fortes. Elle est associée à un déficit marqué en hypocrétine, un neuropeptide de l’hypothalamus essentiel à la régulation de l’éveil et du sommeil.

Jusqu’ici, la forte association de la maladie avec l’allèle HLA-DQB1*06:02 a largement soutenu l’idée d’un mécanisme auto-immun détruisant les neurones à hypocrétine. Cette interprétation reste toutefois débattue. Les chercheurs proposent désormais qu’une altération épigénétique puisse désactiver HCRT et éventuellement d’autres gènes codant des neuropeptides hypothalamiques, sans nécessairement entraîner la disparition complète des neurones concernés.

Cette hypothèse pourrait avoir des conséquences thérapeutiques majeures: si les neurones sont toujours présents mais fonctionnellement silencieux, leur activité pourrait théoriquement être restaurée. Cette piste est explorée dans le projet Innosuisse 119.682 IP-LS, intitulé « Proof-of-concept of narcolepsy reversal by epigenetic therapy », dirigé scientifiquement par l’Université de Lausanne.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/narcolepsie-une-nouvelle-hypothese-ouvre-la-voie-a-des-traitements-potentiellement-reversibles/

articles.headline: Five destinations, five hair solutions: Schwarzkopf’s holiday pitch
articles.dek: Five destinations, five products: Schwarzkopf turns the Golden Week getaway into haircare marketing.
articles.summary: Schwarzkopf’s holiday campaign with Chinese National Geography pairs five products with five destinations, using salon pop-ups, AI colour previews and stamp collecting to pull in tourists.

cover.alt: A campaign poster of a woman with red hair against a night cityscape

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Five destinations give five products distinct roles, linking haircare and styling to holiday conditions and local aesthetics
• Salon activations turn sightseeing into product discovery, with AI colour previews, scalp assessments and stamp collection for samples and merchandise
• The campaign builds on Schwarzkopf’s China localisation strategy, extending its earlier city-flower roadshow into travel-themed storytelling

In China, the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday is travel season. Tourists flood major cities and historic sites. Schwarzkopf (施华蔻) wants a slice of the action. To get it, they’ve collaborated with Chinese National Geography magazine (中国国家地理) – no connection to the US National Geographic.
The campaign, CITY ATTACK 7.0, pairs five haircare and styling products with Chinese destinations. The idea is to bring washing, care, colouring and styling under one travel-themed idea.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/中国彩｜斐丝丽树莓红棕染发霜_1_施华蔻Schwarzkopf_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/施华蔻Schwarzkopf

blocks.text: Each destination is tied to a role in travellers’ holiday looks. Some connections are practical. Sea breezes in Zhejiang’s Zhoushan islands work as a testing ground for OSiS+ styling spray’s hold claims.
Dry, windy surroundings at Datong’s Hanging Temple frame the brand’s repair shampoo. Others focus on appearance: raspberry reddish-brown hair dye complements Chongqing’s neon nightscape.

The remaining pairings match ONEPUSH hair dye with Hongcun’s traditional architecture and caviar scalp-care shampoo with Shanghai’s Anfu Road. Beyond scenery, the ads incorporate Schwarzkopf’s head silhouette imagery framed against the landscapes.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/中国蓬｜OSiS发胶定型喷雾_1_施华蔻Schwarzkopf_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Schwarzkopf’s holiday
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/施华蔻Schwarzkopf

blocks.text: Salon activations accompany. Mirrors that use AI to preview a hair-colouring are probably the most attention-grabbing element of these. Scalp assessments and a wind challenge are also part of the package.

None of this would be complete without merch, and Schwarzkopf has linked their merch in a way that doesn’t feel forced: tourists are encouraged to collect stamps at the salon activations. Those who complete a collection can redeem samples and the merchandise. It’s a nice route between holiday photograph taking and exploring a haircare need.
Dao View: Give the scenery a job

So where does the idea come from? Schwarzkopf has had a long-running interest in local identity. Its 2025 roadshow paired hairstyles with local flowers in 12 Chinese cities. This travel-linked campaign fits that theme nicely. It’s a logical next step and makes a link-up with Chinese National Geography feel right.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/news/schwarzkopf-holiday-pitch/

articles.headline: Oddly Satisfying Video of Cleaning the Leshan Giant Buddha Raises Eyebrows
articles.dek: A viral clip of workers cleaning the giant statue’s ears and nose turned out to be AI.
articles.summary: A viral clip of workers pulling pigeons and leaves from the Leshan Giant Buddha’s ears was debunked as AI-generated by the site’s managers, a sign of how easily fakes now spread.

cover.alt: The Leshan Giant Buddha carved into a red cliff surrounded by greenery

blocks.text: Carved out of a cliff face during the Tang dynasty, the Leshan Giant Buddha is a marvel of ancient engineering. Sitting 71 meters (233 feet) tall at the confluence of the Min, Dadu, and Qingyi rivers in Sichuan, China, it is the largest and tallest stone Buddha statue in the world. Naturally, an undertaking like cleaning a monument of this scale sounds fascinating.

blocks.alt: RADII highlights the fake viral social video of the Leshan Giant Buddha being cleaned, which turned out to be AI-generated.
blocks.caption: Image via Instagram/capra311.

blocks.text: Recently, a short video began circulating across social media platforms showing maintenance workers dangling from ropes, seemingly “picking” the ears and nose of the Giant Buddha. The clips showed workers pulling out pigeons, leaves, and debris from the statue’s massive crevices, with monkeys playfully stealing hard hats nearby. The footage quickly went viral, captivating viewers with its hyper-realistic look.
There’s just one problem: none of it is real.

blocks.alt: RADII highlights the fake viral social video of the Leshan Giant Buddha being cleaned, which turned out to be AI-generated.
blocks.caption: Speculation online over the authenticity of the video has started to spread. Image via DigitEye.

blocks.text: The Leshan Giant Buddha Management Committee swiftly debunked the video, confirming that the entire clip was generated by AI. It’s a glaring example of a troubling trend in digital culture: the rise of “AI slop.” As artificial intelligence tools become more advanced and accessible, it is becoming increasingly difficult for the average user to distinguish authentic footage from fabricated content.

blocks.alt: RADII highlights the fake viral social video of the Leshan Giant Buddha being cleaned, which turned out to be AI-generated.
blocks.caption: Image via Wild Great Wall.

blocks.text: This phenomenon is exacerbated by the explosion of bot accounts that churn out fake, clickbait videos masquerading as cultural or educational content. Designed purely for engagement farming and doomscrolling, these short clips offer no genuine historical context or benefit. Instead, they warp reality and exploit heritage sites for cheap views. As we navigate this new digital landscape, keeping a critical eye on our feeds has never been more essential.
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/leshan-giant-buddha-ai-video-slop

articles.headline: Nobel de médecine 2026 : la lumière au service de la compréhension du cerveau
articles.dek: News · 7 octobre 2026
articles.summary: Le Nobel de médecine 2026 distingue Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann et Georg Nagel pour l’optogénétique, qui permet d’allumer ou d’éteindre des neurones avec de la lumière.

cover.alt: Portrait du neuroscientifique Karl Deisseroth, l’un des trois lauréats
cover.credit: Photo: Christopher Michel / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.text: Le prix Nobel de physiologie ou médecine 2026 a été attribué à Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann et Georg Nagel pour leurs travaux pionniers sur l’optogénétique, une technique qui permet de contrôler l’activité des cellules nerveuses grâce à la lumière. Cette approche a profondément transformé l’étude du cerveau et de ses circuits.

Les recherches de Peter Hegemann et Georg Nagel ont notamment conduit à l’identification de la channelrhodopsine, une protéine sensible à la lumière découverte chez une algue unicellulaire. Karl Deisseroth a ensuite adapté ce mécanisme aux neurones, ouvrant la possibilité de les activer ou de les inhiber avec une grande précision. Cette méthode permet aujourd’hui aux scientifiques d’étudier les circuits impliqués dans la mémoire, les émotions, les comportements ou encore certaines maladies neurologiques et psychiatriques.

Les trois chercheurs sont associés à plusieurs grandes institutions scientifiques. Karl Deisseroth travaille à l’Université Stanford et au Howard Hughes Medical Institute, tandis que Peter Hegemann est professeur à l’Université Humboldt de Berlin et Georg Nagel à l’Université de Wurtzbourg. Une partie déterminante des découvertes récompensées a également été réalisée dans des instituts de la Société Max-Planck en Allemagne.

Le comité Nobel du Karolinska Institutet estime que l’optogénétique a ouvert une nouvelle ère pour les neurosciences. Au-delà de la recherche fondamentale, cette technologie nourrit aussi des perspectives thérapeutiques, notamment pour certaines déficiences visuelles et pour une meilleure compréhension des maladies du cerveau.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/nobel-de-medecine-2026-la-lumiere-au-service-de-la-comprehension-du-cerveau/
Cover image: Christopher Michel / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

articles.headline: ROSÉ fronts Levi’s Beijing pop-up and a premium denim push
articles.dek: Levi’s ends its touring denim market in Beijing with ROSÉ pieces and a premium BLUE TAB line.
articles.summary: Levi’s brought its touring denim market to Beijing with ROSÉ collaboration pieces, the premium BLUE TAB line and local customisation, as it pushes into womenswear and upmarket.

cover.alt: Denim jackets and jeans displayed on a wooden stand at a Levi’s pop-up

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Levi’s Beijing pop-up brings together ROSÉ’s collaboration, denim heritage and premium collections to support its womenswear and upmarket ambitions
• BLUE TAB showcases Levi’s move beyond jeans into a premium wardrobe, drawing on Japanese craftsmanship
• Beijing-exclusive customisation, craft workshops and local refreshments give the touring format a connection to the city

Levi’s has brought its touring denim market to Beijing’s WF Central. It’s the final stop after Shanghai and Chengdu stops, and two spheres Levi’s is looking to grow. That means ROSÉ collaboration pieces to push womenswear, and a new premium collection for a higher-end rail.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/北京丹宁市集抢先逛，玩转攻略先收好_3_Levis中国_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Levi’s Beijing pop-up
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/Levis中国

blocks.text: The global brand ambassador’s collection has its own display area. Pieces feature back patches bearing LEVI STRAUSS WITH ROSÉ in her handwriting. Fans can personalise them with motifs including ‘number one girl’, the opening track on her debut album rosie, and 11. That number, a reference to her birthday.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/北京丹宁市集抢先逛，玩转攻略先收好_5_Levis中国_来自小红书网页版-1024x682.jpg
blocks.alt: Levi’s Beijing pop-up

blocks.text: The partnership supports a growing business segment: Levi’s womenswear sales rose 11% globally in its second quarter of 2026. Asia is also a focus for its experiential marketing. ROSÉ-linked women’s events and collaboration clothing have been pushed in major Asian cities from Tokyo to Seoul as well as the aforementioned Shanghai and Chengdu.

Elsewhere in the pop-up Levi’s Vintage Clothing follows the evolution of the 501 range through a history wall. The BLUE TAB – Levi’s new premium line – Autumn/Winter 2026 collection also gets a display. Introduced for Spring/Summer 2025, the line is part of Levi’s move upmarket, drawing on Japanese craftsmanship to expand its denim proposition.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ROSE_4_合肥万象城Levis_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/合肥万象城Levis

blocks.text: Beijing’s contribution comes through participation. At the Tailor Shop, visitors can try metallic heat transfers, embroidery and screen printing with artist-designed, Beijing-exclusive graphics. Denim workshops incorporate local folk art, while community brand Tiaohai (跳海) serves drinks from a vintage American-style trailer. Beijing snacks round out the day.
Dao view: Levi want more reasons for denim to sell

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ROSE_2_合肥万象城Levis_来自小红书网页版-1.jpg

blocks.text: The pop-up brings several commercial ambitions together. ROSÉ gives fans a reason to visit, the archives establish denim expertise, and BLUE TAB introduces a more premium wardrobe. Local customisation connects these global propositions to Beijing.
This is a push into the expanding womenswear segment, and the Asian market at a time when both are becoming important segments for the famed American denim brand.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/news/levis-beijing-pop-up/

articles.headline: Skate of the Art: How This Shanghai Museum Presents Skateboarding’s Visual History
articles.dek: Fotografiska Shanghai traces skateboarding’s visual history, from Venice Beach pools to China’s streets.
articles.summary: Skate of the Art at Fotografiska Shanghai brings together more than 20 photographers to trace skate culture from 1970s California to China, now one of its newest scenes.

cover.alt: An exhibition poster showing a skateboarder mid-air above bold yellow lettering

blocks.text: What’s the first thing that comes to mind when you think about skateboarding? Probably an Ollie or Kickflip. And what’s the backdrop? Probably LA, maybe an empty pool in Venice Beach, or a kid getting kicked out of a parking lot somewhere in the Valley. Most likely it’s not a scene within China. Complicating that picture is Skate of the Art: Skateboarding Across Cultures, an exhibition that’s currently on view at Fotografiska Shanghai through October 25.

Skateboarding has always been more than a sport; it’s an attitude, a visual code, a whole aesthetic economy. And photography has been welded to it from the start, turning a bunch of kids on planks with wheels into one of the most recognizable youth cultures on the planet. Skate of the Art sits at that intersection, pulling together more than twenty photographers and artists from five continents to trace skate culture frame by frame: from Hugh Holland’s sun-bleached, empty pool in California during the 1970s, through Larry Clark’s unflinching youth-culture grit and Ed Templeton’s diary-style intimacy, all the way to the present.

blocks.caption: Rooftop Landscape with skaters Marcus, Saizhi, Brian, Per, in Shanghai (2018), shot by Jedi Zhou.

blocks.text: That present, increasingly, runs through China. Over the past decade, the country has become one of the newest skate scenes, and the exhibition gives it a space to prove this point. Alongside the genre’s most iconic image on Chinese soil—Mike Blabac’s 2005 photo of Danny Way jumping the Great Wall—a stunt that beamed China into skateboarding’s global visual memory almost by accident, Skate of the Art stacks up work from a new generation of local photographers. You’ve got Jedi Zhou tracing skaters through Shanghai’s traffic and skyscrapers, Jeff Yiu’s years-long documentary project on Beijing’s scene, Bilal’s street-style portraits of Shanghai skater Pi Kai, and Terry Xie’s images of Tsring, the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau’s only pro skater who travels three days and a thousand kilometers just to skate with other people on Skateboard Day in Lhasa.

Seen together, it’s less a story about skateboarding’s Western origins with China tacked on at the end, and more a reminder that skate culture has always grown its own roots wherever it lands. To learn more about how the show came together, RADII spoke with Skate of the Art‘s curator Nadine Barth.
RADII: This exhibition treats skate photography as visual culture rather than sports documentation. What made Shanghai the right place to make that argument?

Nadine Barth: Shanghai is a modern, cosmopolitan city. I expanded my original concept to include Asian photographic perspectives, which greatly benefited the exhibition. I hadn’t previously been familiar with artists like Jedi Zhou or Bilal; discovering their visual strength was an exciting experience for me. And a venue like Fotografiska—which showcases lifestyle phenomena at its other locations as well—is the ideal setting to present the aesthetically inspiring world of skateboarding.

The show spans fifty years and five continents—from Hugh Holland’s 1970s California pool photography to work being made today in Shanghai and on the Tibetan plateau. Do you see that as one continuous visual language traveling across time and geography, or as separate local stories? And how do you think something like this impacts the China of today?

There is a beautiful correspondence between the styles of Hugh Holland and Marcel Veldman, despite the more than forty years separating them: we see a similar softness and elegance in their choice of imagery, and an affectionate use of black and white that takes on a narrative quality. Spanning the intervening years up to the present day, we encounter the full range of what photography can achieve: classic portraits, sweeping landscape tableaux, technical experiments such as panoramas and fisheye lenses, studies of speed, and storytelling. It is the combination of these diverse forms of expression that creates the complete picture — one that resonates on multiple levels.

I wouldn’t presume to judge what kind of impact this complex visual narrative might have on China. However, I would like to see skateboard photography recognized as a form of artistic expression in the future.

The Danny Way Great Wall photo is probably skateboarding’s most famous image in China, but it’s an outsider’s stunt on a monument. You’re placing it against Jedi Zhou, who’s shooting his own city from the inside. What does that contrast bring up for you?

After all, we can best understand a phenomenon by viewing it from as many angles as possible—not just from the inside and the outside, but also as a singular entity in relation to the broader context. The complexity of Skate of the Art fits seamlessly into Fotografiska’s spectrum of diverse approaches to both contemporary and historical photography. I think it is fantastic that, within Skate of the Art, we are able to showcase fifty years of visual power from such varied perspectives.

blocks.caption: A shot by Mike Blabac of the landing ramp for the iconic Danny Way Great Wall photo.

blocks.text: The only professional skater on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau travels three days just to reach a gathering in Lhasa. What does that story tell about what skateboarding means to someone practicing it where there’s no scene at all?

The story shows that you can skateboard anywhere in the world—even alone. It involves shifting your focus between yourself and your board, your skills, and your surroundings. And then, of course, it is wonderful to experience the opposite: meeting up with other skaters in Lhasa for Skateboard Day. My favorite image from the exhibition is the photo of the seven skateboards in the square—abstract, yet emotional at the same time.

Skaters claiming streets and plazas read differently in China, where public space is governed differently than in the West. How does that change what it means for a teenager to skate through it, and for a photographer to document that?
I can speak here only as a curator who is delighted when a photographer has managed to capture those rare moments—such as night-time skating—in evocative images.
What would you love to see happen in Shanghai as a result of this exhibition—beyond the walls of the museum, in how skaters are seen and treated in public space?

It would be great if skateboarding were viewed as an expression of the joy of living and if there were more places where it could be practiced officially. And, of course, if many more people bought a board and simply started rolling…
All images via Fotografiska.
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/skate-of-the-art-shanghai-museum-skateboarding-visual-history

articles.headline: Les autres deviennent meilleurs…
articles.dek: News · 1er octobre 2026
articles.summary: L’ETH Zurich et l’EPFL reculent d’un rang et Tsinghua dépasse l’ETH pour la première fois : pour l’auteur, la Suisse doit mesurer sa progression à la vitesse du reste du monde.

cover.alt: La cour intérieure à arcades du bâtiment principal de l’ETH Zurich

blocks.text: L’ETH Zurich perd une place. L’EPFL aussi. La réaction naturelle serait d’y voir un recul, peut-être même le signe d’un affaiblissement. Je crois qu’il faut regarder les choses autrement. Une place dans un classement n’existe jamais en soi; elle est toujours relative. On peut continuer à progresser, à mieux former, à davantage publier, à renforcer le transfert de technologie, et malgré tout reculer si d’autres avancent plus vite. C’est précisément ce que nous devons apprendre à regarder: non seulement notre propre trajectoire, mais la vitesse du monde autour de nous.

Le fait que Tsinghua dépasse pour la première fois l’ETH Zurich dans le classement du Times Higher Education n’est donc pas une simple anecdote statistique. Pas davantage que la présence désormais affirmée de plusieurs universités asiatiques parmi les toutes premières mondiales. C’est le signe d’un déplacement progressif de la géographie de l’excellence. Pendant longtemps, la Suisse a pu considérer la qualité de ses institutions comme un avantage presque structurel. Mais l’excellence n’est jamais définitivement acquise. Elle n’est pas un patrimoine que l’on conserve intact simplement parce qu’on en a hérité. Elle ressemble davantage à une avance qu’il faut sans cesse recréer, entretenir, remettre en jeu.

La vraie question n’est donc probablement pas de savoir si nous sommes devenus moins bons. Je ne le pense pas. La vraie question est de savoir si nous progressons encore suffisamment vite dans un monde où les autres accélèrent. La Chine, Singapour et, plus largement, une partie de l’Asie investissent avec une intensité remarquable dans la recherche, les infrastructures, les talents et les technologies stratégiques.
