Ce mouvement ne diminue en rien la valeur de nos institutions; il modifie simplement le référentiel dans lequel cette valeur se mesure.

C’est peut-être là que réside le risque le plus subtil pour la Suisse: confondre excellence et avance. Nous pouvons rester excellents tout en perdant progressivement notre avantage relatif. Nous pouvons continuer à faire mieux qu’hier sans pour autant faire mieux que ceux qui nous rattrapent ou nous dépassent. Et dans la recherche comme dans l’innovation, ce ne sont pas nécessairement ceux qui deviennent moins bons qui décrochent. Ce sont parfois simplement ceux qui avancent moins vite que les autres.

L’enjeu n’est donc pas de céder au pessimisme, mais de retrouver le sens du mouvement. Une position n’est jamais un acquis; elle est le résultat provisoire d’un effort, d’une ambition et d’une capacité à se renouveler. Le monde ne nous attend pas.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/les-autres-deviennent-meilleurs/
Cover image: Ximeg / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

articles.headline: Holiday backlash: Are Chinese people getting enough time off?
articles.dek: Make-up working days around National Day have some workers threatening a spending boycott.
articles.summary: China’s make-up working days around National Day sparked a backlash online, with some workers vowing to shun holiday spending and favour firms that offer two-day weekends.

cover.alt: Wooden letter tiles spelling WEEKEND BABY on a white surface
cover.credit: Photo: Sincerely Media / Unsplash, via DAO Insights

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Backlash against make-up working days is prompting some Chinese workers to threaten a boycott of holiday spending
• A WeChat account encouraged consumers to favour businesses offering two-day weekends
• Jinzai and other Chinese brands show how marketing tangible employee benefits can work for a brand

China’s National Day holiday runs from 1-7 October. It’s one of the longer holidays in a Chinese employee’s calendar. This year – as Yili pointed out – it can even be strung together with the Mid-Autumn Festival to make a full 13 days off. But some are questioning just how much of a break they’re getting.

In China, working days are often rearranged to create consecutive days off. It’s called the tiaoxiu (调休) system and it means this year’s holiday comes with two weekend shifts: Sunday 20 September and Saturday 10 October.

blocks.alt: holiday backlash
blocks.caption: Notice from the account reading: ‘Dear friends, please be rational in what you post. Safeguarding national cybersecurity is our shared duty and responsibility. We should consciously uphold it and abide by the rules.’ Image: Rednote

blocks.text: Online, people aren’t happy. A Weibo topic opposing make-up working days attracted 360 million views. Some workers say they will withhold holiday spending in protest. Now their anger is beginning to reach brands.

A WeChat service called Weekend Off Shopping (双休购) surfaced, letting users check whether a business gave employees two-day weekends as a basis for choosing whether to buy from it or not. It drew 150,000 contributors before authorities stepped in and suspended it.

But there’s clearly something in the air. Drinks company, Lu Xiyi (陆喜依) posted a notice announcing 13 consecutive days off over the holiday. Its orders doubled. Snack brand Jinzai (劲仔) offers an example of another approach.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/生日祝福就要发92100000遍！_1_劲仔_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Happy Bday Wang Junkai. In your honour, Jinzai employees get an afternoon off. Images: Rednote/劲仔

blocks.text: To celebrate ambassador Wang Junkai’s birthday (and to much praise) it gave all employees a paid half-day off on 21 September – immediately after that designated working Sunday. It may have been a savvy part of a fan campaign, but it also spoke to a feeling that extended beyond Wang’s followers: people want time away from the grind.
Dao view: When workers’ time off becomes a brand issue
Jinzai isn’t the only brand to pick up on China’s culture of exhausted workers. The aforementioned Yili uses office workers in its campaign films regularly. Other brands employ similar methods.

Overwork is a problem in China. It doesn’t look like it’s going to go away. Often when brands address it, the address comes in the form of marketing. Cynical, you might say, to turn workers’ stress into sales. But in this case the script has been flipped. Now it’s companies that are feeling the pinch.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/news/holiday-backlash-china/

articles.headline: Cyber-Spirituality: How Smart Terminals Are Upgrading Fortune-Telling in Asia
articles.dek: Temples in southern China and Taiwan are swapping fortune-tellers for smart terminals.
articles.summary: Temples in southern China and Taiwan now use smart kiosks to read kau cim fortune sticks, turning a centuries-old ritual into instant, personalised readings on your phone.

cover.alt: A hand holding a smartphone in front of a red Chinese temple

blocks.text: Step into a temple in southern China or Taiwan today, and you might find the scent of incense mingling not with the hushed voices of human fortune-tellers, but with the quiet hum of digital kiosks. Across the region, places of worship are undergoing a quiet cyberpunk revolution, swapping out traditional diviners for smart terminals.

blocks.caption: A temple in Hong Kong that has embraced a digital kiosk for Kau Cim. Image via SCMP.

blocks.text: For centuries, worshippers have sought guidance through kau cim—the ancient practice of shaking a bamboo cylinder until a single fortune stick falls out. Traditionally, a seasoned temple master would interpret the cryptic poem attached to the stick. Now? You just scan a QR code.

blocks.caption: A traditional version of Kau Cim, the Chinese divination practice where you ask a question and draw a numbered bamboo stick from a cylindrical cup to receive guidance. Image via Wikipedia.

blocks.text: Digital kiosks equipped with automated natural language algorithms are stepping in to immediately analyze your custom kau cim results. By cross-referencing ancient texts with localized astrological data, these smart terminals spit out highly personalized, instantly readable fortunes straight to your smartphone. Want to know if your startup will survive the year or if your Hinge date is “the one”? The algorithm has an answer.

While the digitization of religion isn’t entirely a brand new concept—virtual offerings and digital merit boxes have been around for a few years—the integration of NLP and instant data-mapping represents a fascinating evolution. It’s a striking synergy between tech and spirituality, proving that ancient traditions don’t have to resist the future to survive.

For today’s youth, a demographic already deep into embracing astrology, mysticism, and digital convenience, this hybrid approach feels right at home. It demystifies the intimidating temple experience, making ancient wisdom accessible with the simple tap of a screen. Whether it’s the divine or the data speaking, the algorithm is ready to map out your destiny.
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/cyber-spirituality-fortune-telling-smart-terminals

articles.headline: Des OLED imprimables comme des puces électroniques
articles.dek: News · 29 septembre 2026
articles.summary: L’ETH Zurich a mis au point des photoresists électroluminescents qui permettent de graver des OLED par lithographie, comme des puces, pour de futurs micro-écrans ultra-fins.

cover.alt: Gros plan sur les sous-pixels colorés d’un écran OLED
cover.credit: Photo: TECH EDU / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.text: Miniaturiser les écrans OLED est un défi central pour les futurs micro-écrans, la photonique intégrée et certains dispositifs médicaux. Mais les méthodes classiques de fabrication des OLED, comme l’évaporation sous vide ou l’impression jet d’encre, s’accordent mal avec les procédés de lithographie utilisés dans l’industrie des semi-conducteurs.

Une équipe de l’ETH Zurich propose une solution publiée dans Nature: rendre le matériau OLED lui-même compatible avec la lithographie. Les chercheurs ont développé des photoresists électroluminescents, ou ELPR, des polymères capables à la fois d’émettre de la lumière et d’être directement dessinés par lumière ultraviolette ou faisceau d’électrons.

Leur architecture moléculaire est conçue comme un système cœur-coquille. Au centre se trouvent des molécules émettrices, protégées par une enveloppe hôte; à la périphérie, des groupes chimiques permettent la réticulation nécessaire à la lithographie. Cette séparation évite que l’étape de structuration n’endommage la partie lumineuse du matériau.

Les résultats sont prometteurs: l’équipe a réalisé des pixels OLED multicolores par trois cycles successifs de lithographie et a obtenu des motifs fluorescents avec des dimensions critiques descendant jusqu’à 110 nanomètres. Les dispositifs multicolores présentent aussi des rendements quantiques externes supérieurs à 13%, un niveau important pour des OLED directement photolithographiées.

Cette approche pourrait faciliter l’intégration monolithique d’OLED avec des circuits CMOS, ouvrant la voie à des micro-écrans ultrahaute résolution, à des sources lumineuses miniaturisées et à de nouveaux composants optoélectroniques sur puce. Elle ne garantit pas encore une industrialisation immédiate, mais elle montre comment la chimie des matériaux peut rapprocher les OLED du monde des puces électroniques.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/des-oled-imprimables-comme-des-puces-electroniques/
Cover image: TECH EDU / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

articles.headline: Victoria’s Secret returns to Huaihai Road with a rethink of its China stores
articles.dek: Six months after closing its old store, the lingerie brand is back on Shanghai’s Huaihai Road.
articles.summary: Victoria’s Secret has reopened on Shanghai’s Huaihai Road with a flagship that adds fragrance, sportswear and sizing services, as it expands in China while watching each store.

cover.alt: The opening ceremony outside Victoria’s Secret’s new Shanghai flagship

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Victoria’s Secret has returned to Shanghai’s Huaihai Road with a new flagship following its previous store’s closure
• The flagship combines lingerie, sportswear, fragrance and body care with professional sizing services
• Its China retail strategy balances expansion into more cities with greater attention to individual store performance

Victoria’s Secret (维多利亚的秘密) has returned to Shanghai’s Huaihai Road with a new flagship at Longfeng PRSCO. That’s six months after its earlier Lippo Plaza location closed on a case of expired lease. With the return comes a Victoria’s Secret adjusting what its Chinese stores are expected to deliver.

The new shop brings lingerie, loungewear, sportswear, fragrance and body care together. There are now dedicated fragrance and beauty areas and professional sizing services. Store design retains Victoria’s Secret’s signature colours, but now incorporates references to Shanghai’s architecture.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/听说上海最近很容易偶遇维密👀💗_9_Victorias-Secret维多利亚的秘密_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Victoria’s Secret
blocks.caption: Image: Rednote/维多利亚的秘密旗舰店

blocks.text: The brand’s China retail strategy is changing too. It is putting more weight into balancing city coverage with individual-store performance. Regional centres are being targeted for expansion and closer attention is being paid to how each location performs.

But that’s all behind-the-scenes stuff. The Huaihai opening is about giving the full range of Victoria’s Secret products a prominent showcase. As usual, it features practical services to get customers through the door, and that’s the point. The showcase acts as an intro point as much as a point of sale.
Dao view: Can a flagship earn its keep?

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/我们和大家见面啦🥳｜维密旗舰店_1_Mancy～（VS上海管培生版）_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Victoria’s Secret
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote users/Mancy～（VS上海管培生版）/ 当下最需要

blocks.text: A flagship can draw a crowd, but the business still needs shoppers to buy and return. Fragrance and body care could broaden the reasons to visit, while sizing services give lingerie shoppers something useful to seek out in person. The question is how to make a prestigious address best serve everyday demand.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/news/victorias-secret-shanghai-flagship/

articles.headline: Love Letters to Five Cities in China During My Study Abroad Program
articles.dek: A semester abroad, five Chinese cities and a playlist of greatest hits.
articles.summary: A student’s affectionate tour of five Chinese cities visited during a semester abroad, from Chongqing’s neon riverbanks to humid Guangzhou, with must-do tips for each.

cover.alt: The sun setting over misty mountain peaks in China

blocks.text: Far too many university students have tried to capture the magic of studying abroad in words, and while I’ve attempted to resist this perennial urge, I’m finally throwing my hat in the ring. I spent a semester in China frolicking across fields, trekking up mountains, and sprinting from one high-speed train to another. I visited more cities than I can fit here, each deserving its own love letter, so consider this a brief playlist of my semester abroad’s greatest hits.
Chongqing

blocks.alt: RADII writer Nora Lee shares a roundup of her favorite cities in China during her study abroad program.
blocks.caption: Image via RADII/Nora Lee.

blocks.text: After missing our original train and scrambling to find another, my exhausted friends and I arrived in Chongqing primed for disappointment, the words “over-hyped” already on the tips of our tongues. Known as China’s “8-D cyberpunk metropolis,” Chongqing could easily be reduced to its flashing lights and infamous infrastructure, but an intangible sweetness comes from the hodgepodge of elements that make up one of China’s most viral cities. A serenity lies in the river cradled by its surrounding mountains and the towering, mind-bending buildings built into them. It is one of the most densely populated cities in China, and one of its hottest tourist destinations, but somehow, the lights felt like they were shining just for me.
Must-do: River cruise, 18 Steps District (Shibati, 十八梯).
Guangzhou

blocks.alt: RADII writer Nora Lee shares a roundup of her favorite cities in China during her study abroad program.
blocks.caption: Image via RADII/Nora Lee.

blocks.text: In the sweltering, sticky heat of July, my friends and I found solace from Guangzhou’s notorious humidity in its extensive underground shopping centers. One of the final cities I visited during my stint in China, I was determined to eat and shop my way through Guangzhou until my Alipay gave out. But for all the damage the trip did to my wallet, Guangzhou turned out to be so much more than just har-gow and cheap bargains. Over 2,000 years old, Guangzhou has been one of China’s central trade hubs since the founding of the Maritime Silk Road. A highlight for me was the tree-lined pedestrian street on Shamian Island, once a strategic defense point during the Opium Wars and now lined with Qing-era colonial architecture.
Must-do: Canton Tower at night.
Zhangjiajie

blocks.alt: RADII writer Nora Lee shares a roundup of her favorite cities in China during her study abroad program.
blocks.caption: Image via TripAdvisor.

blocks.text: So, I got severe food poisoning on this trip. Tragic, I know. But what comes up must come down. And getting to witness the majesty of Zhangjiajie National Forest Park was, undoubtedly, one of the highs of my life. The sights were too beautiful! The skies were too clear! Tears of wonder streamed too freely! It was only natural that the universe, and my body, would attempt to put things back into equilibrium. I’ll never forget the smell of sweat mingled with the crisp scent of air that can only be found at high altitudes, perfuming the buses as they wound their way up the mountains. Cramped from arm to sticky arm, we collectively craned our heads through the windows to catch glimpses of the view whenever the foliage or cliffside allowed it, as if the Earth were playing peekaboo with us. More than the famous reveal from the top of the Bailong elevator, or the sweeping panoramas of the viewing platforms, it’s these moments I remember most vividly.
Must-do: Golden Whip Stream.
Xiamen

blocks.alt: RADII writer Nora Lee shares a roundup of her favorite cities in China during her study abroad program.
blocks.caption: Image via RADII/Nora Lee.

blocks.text: I spent my final days in China visiting a friend in the idyllic, oceanside city of Xiamen. When I think of Xiamen, I’ll think of balmy days spent on the back of a scooter, and my toes buried into the sand as I listened to the gentle crash of waves. It is a city of warm, breezy nights and sweltering, humid days. Tranquility is its greatest strength. Greenery abounds throughout the city, palm trees line oceanside walkways, and vines race across pastel overpasses. Spending time in Xiamen feels like spending a week bathed in an aesthetic Instagram filter; edges are a little softer, and life’s problems feel like blurred figures in the background.
Must-do: Seafood hot pot at 朱富贵 (Zhū fùguì).
Beijing

blocks.alt: RADII writer Nora Lee shares a roundup of her favorite cities in China during her study abroad program.
blocks.caption: Image via RADII/Nora Lee.

blocks.text: I’m not sure if living in a city for four months strictly counts as a “visit,” but I would be remiss to forgo Beijing on this list. When I first expressed interest in studying abroad in China, I told my mom there were two primary options: Shanghai or Beijing. She said that while the cosmopolitan comforts of Shanghai may be more familiar to me as an American when it comes to culture, history, and unabashed national pride, Beijing reigns supreme.

It’s hard to differentiate whether I fell in love with the city of Beijing or the people who populated it. While I mourn the long subway rides from the Haidian district, where my school’s campus was, to the city center for hutong exploring or to Sanlitun for shopping and nights out, I miss the people who made those hours fly by even more.
Must-do: Beihai Park.

It’s hard to say whether the memories I made in China will stay with me forever. I’d like to think they will, but my memory is notoriously fallible. These cities, these sights, the people, the breeze, the blossoms—these will all move on without me. So before the progression of time inevitably dulls my memories and theirs, this is my attempt to hold on. This, and the monthly bike subscription I’m still paying for because I can’t figure out how to cancel it.
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/5-study-abroad-places-to-visit-in-china

articles.headline: La face cachée de la Lune garde la trace d’un ancien champ magnétique
articles.dek: News · 29 septembre 2026
articles.summary: Sous la région de Dewar, sur la face cachée de la Lune, l’ETH Zurich a repéré un basalte enfoui fortement aimanté, signe que la Lune a jadis eu un champ magnétique.

cover.alt: Une planète bleue et verte sur fond de ciel noir
cover.credit: Photo: BoliviaInteligente / Unsplash, via Republic of Innovation

blocks.text: La Lune n’a plus aujourd’hui de champ magnétique global comme celui de la Terre. Pourtant, certaines régions de sa croûte restent fortement aimantées, comme si elles avaient enregistré un champ disparu depuis longtemps. Une étude menée notamment par l’ETH Zurich apporte un nouvel indice sur cette ancienne histoire magnétique.

Les chercheurs se sont intéressés à la région de Dewar, sur la face cachée de la Lune. Cette zone présente à la fois une anomalie magnétique intense et un « swirl », une formation claire en surface dont l’origine intrigue depuis des décennies. En combinant des observations magnétiques et gravimétriques, l’équipe a reconstruit la structure du sous-sol lunaire dans cette région.

Le résultat pointe vers un corps peu profond, dense et fortement aimanté, compatible avec du basalte de mare enfoui, c’est-à-dire une ancienne roche volcanique lunaire. Selon les chercheurs, cette roche aurait été magnétisée au moment de son refroidissement, en présence d’un champ magnétique lunaire actif.

L’intensité nécessaire dépasse 11 microteslas, ce qui suggère qu’une dynamo lunaire fonctionnait encore il y a environ 4,2 milliards d’années. Cette conclusion est importante, car la durée de vie de l’ancien champ magnétique lunaire reste débattue: les échantillons rapportés par les missions Apollo donnent des signaux parfois difficiles à interpréter, tandis que les données orbitales montrent des anomalies dont l’origine peut être multiple.

L’étude éclaire aussi la formation des swirls lunaires. Dans le cas de Dewar, leur apparition semble nécessiter une aimantation horizontale et des matériaux enrichis en oxydes de fer. Ces résultats ne résolvent pas toute l’histoire magnétique de la Lune, mais ils relient pour la première fois cette anomalie à une origine géologique précise. Pour les futures missions lunaires, Dewar pourrait devenir une cible clé pour comprendre comment la Lune a perdu son champ magnétique.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/la-face-cachee-de-la-lune-garde-la-trace-dun-ancien-champ-magnetique/

articles.headline: Mithridate adopts London club for the Fashion Week runway
articles.dek: The Guangzhou brand mines 1980s London club culture for its Spring 2027 show.
articles.summary: Guangzhou-founded Mithridate drew on London’s 1980s club culture for its Spring 2027 show, pairing British references with Chinese craftsmanship as it targets European markets.

cover.alt: A model in profile with slicked hair against a black background

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Mithridate’s Spring 2027 collection draws on London’s 1980s club culture to sharpen its British creative identity
• The Guangzhou-founded brand is pairing London cultural references with Chinese craftsmanship as it targets European markets

Guangzhou-founded Mithridate looked to a very different city for its spring/summer 2027 collection. At London Fashion Week, British creative director Daniel Fletcher presented a collection that draws on the city’s 1980s club culture. The idea is to give the brand a London edge as it looks to open up new markets in Europe.

Fletcher’s approach here isn’t too much of a departure. Fletcher has described Mithridate as a brand inspired by British heritage and infused with Chinese craftsmanship. The clubbing reference goes a bit further in the British direction though. It also fine tunes the scope. What was the broad stroke of British tailoring is now given a more particular piece of London’s cultural history to work from.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/27春夏时装秀丨色彩张力_1_MITHRIDATE_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Mithridate
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/MITHRIDATE

blocks.text: Fletcher’s London references have a clear connection to his own life and work. Mithridate’s challenge is to make them feel like part of a recognisable brand identity. It must also fit that around its Guangzhou roots and its Chinese manufacturing identity.
Dao view: Can the runway story sell the clothes?

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/27春夏时装秀丨色彩张力_4_MITHRIDATE_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/MITHRIDATE

blocks.text: London Fashion Week introduces Mithridate to international press and buyers, but it’s just an introduction. Fletcher has said physical stores matter because customers need to handle the clothes. They need to try them on and judge their quality. He wants that experience to challenge assumptions about Chinese manufacturing.

So, there’s a commercial test and a cultural one. Mithridate’s London nightlife look can catch the attention it wants from European markets, but the brands will need stores on the ground to show customers what the Mithridate stands for.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/news/mithridate-london-fashion-week/

articles.headline: Porcelain Poetry: LEMAIRE Turns Chinese Craft Into Everyday Art
articles.dek: The Parisian house’s first artist collaboration turns jade porcelain trays into wall art.
articles.summary: LEMAIRE’s first object collaboration, Gathering Plates, pairs Chengdu artists AiHeMei and Li Qing on three signed jade porcelain trays that also hang on the wall as paintings.

cover.alt: A white wall and doorway framed by greenery at a LEMAIRE space

blocks.text: There is something very LEMAIRE about making a beautiful object that you can also put snacks on.

blocks.alt: RADII features french quiet luxury brand LEMAIRE's Fall/Winter 2026 campaign and 'Gathering Plates' collaboration with photographer and painter AiHeMei (Xu Jing) and ceramic artist Li Qing.
blocks.caption: Image via LEMAIRE.

blocks.text: For Fall/Winter 2026, the Parisian fashion house known for its soft tailoring, muted palette, excellent bags, and general refusal to be too loud about anything is expanding its world beyond clothes. Its new series of artist collaborations focuses on objects for everyday life, with the first project, Gathering Plates, bringing together Chengdu-based photographer and painter AiHeMei (Xu Jing) and ceramic artist Li Qing.

blocks.alt: RADII features french quiet luxury brand LEMAIRE's Fall/Winter 2026 campaign and 'Gathering Plates' collaboration with photographer and painter AiHeMei (Xu Jing) and ceramic artist Li Qing.
blocks.caption: (Left) Photographer and painter, AiHeMei (Xu Jing); (Right) ceramic artist and director of the Shushan Kiln Ceramic Art Museum, Li Qing. Image via LEMAIRE.

blocks.text: The result is three handmade jade porcelain trays—月华花 (yuèhuá huā, “Moonlight Flower”), 秋痕 (qiū hén, “Traces of Autumn”), and 月梢 (yuè shāo, “Moon Above the Treetops”). They are designed to sit somewhere between tableware and art objects: lay them flat and they work as serving trays; prop them upright and they become paintings you can hang. And for a personal touch, each is individually signed by the artists.

blocks.alt: RADII features french quiet luxury brand LEMAIRE's Fall/Winter 2026 campaign and 'Gathering Plates' collaboration with photographer and painter AiHeMei (Xu Jing) and ceramic artist Li Qing.
blocks.caption: LEMAIRE’s three handmade jade porcelain trays for its Gathering Plates collaboration. Image via LEMAIRE.

blocks.text: It is a neat little summary of what makes LEMAIRE interesting in the first place. Founded by Christophe Lemaire in 1991 and now led by Lemaire and Sarah-Linh Tran, the house has built its reputation around clothing that is understated without being boring—pieces designed to be worn, layered, lived in, and gradually made your own. Its interest in craftsmanship and everyday function makes a porcelain plate feel right at home—both at a LEMAIRE flagship boutique and in your own living room.
In China, that idea gets particularly interesting.
Welcome to the LEMAIRE House

The Gathering Plates project has been chosen to be presented at LEMAIRE’s Wukang boutique in Shanghai, as well as its Beijing and Chengdu stores. The Shanghai space is a particularly fitting home for the project: rather than operating like a conventional luxury store, the Wukang boutique has been conceived as a lived-in environment where clothes share space with furniture, books, music, ceramics, and other objects.

blocks.alt: RADII features french quiet luxury brand LEMAIRE's Fall/Winter 2026 campaign and 'Gathering Plates' collaboration with photographer and painter AiHeMei (Xu Jing) and ceramic artist Li Qing.
blocks.caption: LEMAIRE’s beautifully crafted flagship Wukang boutique in Shanghai. Image via LEMAIRE.

blocks.text: That domestic feeling is central to LEMAIRE’s approach. The brand has long treated the home as an extension of its creative universe—somewhere clothing, design, art, and the rituals of daily life can overlap.

The Wukang boutique pushes that idea into a distinctly Shanghai context. Located in a historic building on Wukang Road, the space mixes European design pieces with vintage objects sourced locally, creating something that feels closer to a stylish collector’s apartment than a traditional fashion retail environment.
That makes Gathering Plates feel less like an art collaboration dropped into a store and more like something the space was waiting for.

Li Qing has previously created ceramic pieces for LEMAIRE boutiques and offices around the world, while AiHeMei contributed to A Box of Impressions, a photography project presented for the opening of LEMAIRE’s Palais Royal space in Paris. The two artists therefore arrive at Gathering Plates with existing relationships to the house—but their collaboration here is firmly rooted in Chinese craft and contemporary artistic practice.

blocks.alt: RADII features french quiet luxury brand LEMAIRE's Fall/Winter 2026 campaign and 'Gathering Plates' collaboration with photographer and painter AiHeMei (Xu Jing) and ceramic artist Li Qing.
blocks.caption: Images via LEMAIRE.

blocks.text: Two Artists, One Very Good Plate

AiHeMei, also known as Xu Jing, is a Chengdu-based visual artist whose practice moves between traditional Chinese painting, oil painting, watercolor, and photography. Her background spans jurisprudence, art, and design, and that mix shows up in her interest in pictorial composition — essentially, how an image can be structured, balanced, and made to feel alive.

blocks.alt: RADII features french quiet luxury brand LEMAIRE's Fall/Winter 2026 campaign and 'Gathering Plates' collaboration with photographer and painter AiHeMei (Xu Jing) and ceramic artist Li Qing.
blocks.caption: The works of AiHeMei, AKA Xu Jing. Images via LEMAIRE.

blocks.text: For Gathering Plates, she turns botanical forms into abstract compositions, using a delicate palette of colors across the porcelain surfaces. The result isn’t a literal painting of flowers or leaves. Instead, natural forms become shapes, gestures, and fragments.

blocks.alt: RADII features french quiet luxury brand LEMAIRE's Fall/Winter 2026 campaign and 'Gathering Plates' collaboration with photographer and painter AiHeMei (Xu Jing) and ceramic artist Li Qing.
blocks.caption: The works of AiHeMei, AKA Xu Jing. Images via LEMAIRE.

blocks.text: Then the kiln gets involved.

Li Qing, a Chengdu-based ceramic artist and director of the Shushan Kiln Ceramic Art Museum, brings a different kind of expertise. His practice connects traditional craftsmanship with contemporary design, working across porcelain painting, ceramic-making, and firing. A recurring concern in his work is the relationship between material, form, and function—which is pretty much the entire brief for a plate that wants to moonlight as a piece of art.

blocks.alt: RADII features french quiet luxury brand LEMAIRE's Fall/Winter 2026 campaign and 'Gathering Plates' collaboration with photographer and painter AiHeMei (Xu Jing) and ceramic artist Li Qing.
blocks.caption: The works of Li Qing. Images via LEMAIRE.

blocks.text: For these three works, Li handles the physical alchemy: modelling, drying, grinding, two-layer glazing, and double firing. AiHeMei’s paintings are applied to the porcelain, where the firing process subtly alters the color and texture of her compositions.

blocks.alt: RADII features french quiet luxury brand LEMAIRE's Fall/Winter 2026 campaign and 'Gathering Plates' collaboration with photographer and painter AiHeMei (Xu Jing) and ceramic artist Li Qing.
blocks.caption: The works of Li Qing. Images via LEMAIRE.

blocks.text: So what arrives at the end isn’t simply an image transferred onto a ceramic surface. The material has had its own say.

That is where the collaboration gets particularly satisfying. AiHeMei’s visual language and Li’s ceramic practice don’t just sit beside one another—they change one another. Painting becomes ceramic; ceramic becomes painting; an object intended for the dining table becomes something you might want to put on a wall.

blocks.alt: RADII features french quiet luxury brand LEMAIRE's Fall/Winter 2026 campaign and 'Gathering Plates' collaboration with photographer and painter AiHeMei (Xu Jing) and ceramic artist Li Qing.
blocks.caption: Final touches on the final result; the work of AiHeMei and Li Qing. Image via LEMAIRE.

blocks.text: A Quieter Kind of Cultural Exchange
There is a tendency for global fashion brands to approach Chinese culture with the subtlety of a neon sign. LEMAIRE’s approach here is considerably quieter.

Rather than simply borrowing a recognizable Chinese motif, Gathering Plates is interested in the people, materials, and techniques behind the object. Its Chinese-ness isn’t reduced to decoration. It comes through the artists’ practices, the use of porcelain, the relationship with botanical imagery, and the long, slightly obsessive process required to make each piece.
That feels particularly appropriate for a French house whose whole aesthetic is built around restraint.

blocks.caption: AiHeMei documenting Li Qing during their collaboration. Image via LEMAIRE.

blocks.text: LEMAIRE has increasingly developed relationships with Chinese artists and cultural traditions as its presence in the country has grown. Its Chengdu, Shanghai, and Beijing spaces have provided settings for collaborations and objects that connect the house’s global design language with local creative practices. The brand has also explored Chinese cultural moments such as Qixi and Lunar New Year through its collections and storytelling.

Gathering Plates takes that interest somewhere even more tactile. Instead of putting Chinese culture onto a runway and sending it back out into the world six months later, the project places it in the home, or, at least, in LEMAIRE’s very stylish approximation of one.
And perhaps that is the most appealing part.
Porcelain is meant to be touched. A tray can carry fruit, tea, flowers, snacks, keys, or whatever else ends up accumulating on a table. Art doesn’t necessarily have to sit behind glass to matter.

The three plates draw on botanical forms, the harvest, abundance, and the changing seasons. But you don’t need to know your qiū hén from your yuè shāo to get the point. These are objects about slowing down, noticing materials, and making the ordinary slightly more beautiful.
Which, honestly, sounds like a pretty good reason to put down the phone and set the table.
Gathering Plates is presented at LEMAIRE‘s Wukang, Beijing, and Chengdu boutiques until October 7.
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/porcelain-poetry-lemaire-turns-chinese-craft-into-everyday-art

articles.headline: Aux sources du Système solaire
articles.dek: News · 29 septembre 2026
articles.summary: Les isotopes de fer, de titane et de chrome des échantillons de Bennu révèlent un astéroïde hybride, mêlant des matériaux du Système solaire interne et externe.

cover.alt: Mosaïque de l’astéroïde Bennu prise par la sonde OSIRIS-REx
cover.credit: Photo: NASA/Goddard/University of Arizona / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

blocks.text: L’astéroïde Bennu continue de livrer ses secrets. Grâce aux échantillons rapportés sur Terre par la mission OSIRIS-REx de la NASA, une équipe menée notamment par l’ETH Zurich propose un nouveau scénario pour expliquer l’origine de ce corps primitif, riche en eau et en matière organique.

Les chercheurs ont analysé la composition isotopique du fer, du titane et du chrome dans de minuscules fragments de Bennu. Ces signatures chimiques fonctionnent comme des archives: elles permettent de remonter aux réservoirs de poussières présents au moment de la formation du Système solaire, il y a environ 4,5 milliards d’années.

Les résultats montrent que Bennu ressemble fortement à Ryugu, un autre astéroïde dont des échantillons ont été rapportés par la mission japonaise Hayabusa2, ainsi qu’aux météorites carbonées de type CI. Mais cette parenté ne pointe pas vers une origine simple. Bennu apparaît plutôt comme un « hybride », combinant des matériaux associés au Système solaire interne et externe.

Selon le scénario proposé, ces corps se seraient formés près de la ligne des glaces, là où la vapeur d’eau pouvait se condenser en glace. À cette époque, la croissance rapide de Jupiter aurait freiné le passage de grosses particules, tout en laissant circuler et se mélanger des poussières plus fines. Ce tri naturel aurait permis la formation d’objets chimiquement proches de la composition globale du Soleil, tout en conservant une richesse en eau et en carbone.

Ces travaux ne racontent pas seulement l’histoire de Bennu. Ils aident aussi à comprendre comment les matériaux ayant contribué à la formation des planètes rocheuses, dont la Terre, ont circulé dans le jeune Système solaire. Les prochaines missions de retour d’échantillons, notamment vers Phobos, pourraient préciser encore cette carte des origines.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/aux-sources-du-systeme-solaire/
Cover image: NASA/Goddard/University of Arizona / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

articles.headline: Haier makes campaign content from repairing a 1997 dishwasher
articles.dek: Haier restored a blogger’s 1997 dishwasher and turned the repair into a campaign.
articles.summary: Haier shipped a blogger’s broken 1997 Little Seashell dishwasher to its Qingdao factory, restored it with archive parts and finishes, and turned the after-sales service into a campaign.

cover.alt: Haier engineers examining a vintage white dishwasher at a workbench

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Haier restored a blogger’s 1997 Little Seashell dishwasher and turned the exceptional after-sales service into campaign content
• Resurfacing the original advert connected Haier’s product heritage with contemporary concerns about appliance durability and customer support
• Online praise for the old model’s layout gave Haier unsolicited product feedback

Chinese home appliance brand Haier (海尔) nailed a customer interaction moment, bringing a run-down dishwasher back from the dead. The machine – a Little Seashell (小海贝) model that dates back to 1997 – belonged to a blogger who mentioned the breakage online. Haier shipped the dishwasher back to its Qingdao factory and gave it a full restoration.

It was no small job, but Haier went the distance. They had to source replacement parts from unused displays and install a bunch of new bits too. They even consulted their archives to recreate the original matt finish and produced a manual combining the old cover with updated instructions.

Once all this was done, Haier pushed the repair story into its marketing. The brand resurfaced the Little Seashell’s original 1997 advertisement, where the promise of ‘freeing your hands’ paints dishwashing technology as a futuristic vision of domestic bliss.
Footage of the blogger’s restored Little Seashell dishwasher played alongside the old ad in a bit of campaigning that hit nostalgically at elements of the brand’s heritage.

Of course, none of this went unnoticed online. Social media users chimed in to ask for their own products to be refurbished. But perhaps most interestingly, discussion began to praise Haier’s older appliances over its new ones.
The Dao view: You never know where the internet might take things

What’s smart about Haier’s move here is that home appliances are often billed as durable before they have a chance to demonstrate it. This tactic gives Haier an opportunity to show that their machines, with a bit of love and care, can stand up to the brand’s durability claims.

Haier’s idea was also solid on the social-media front. The story had enough behind it that it was all but sure to spark online engagement. The funny thing is you just never know where that engagement might go. In this case, Haier discovered that some users prefer older designs to their newer ones. Feedback wasn’t what they were looking for, but it’s what they got. Perhaps we’ll see it implemented in a future campaign…
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/news/haier-dishwasher-repair-campaign/

articles.headline: Who is Fang Taozi and Why is China At Odds Over Her?
articles.dek: An AI-generated actress is winning Chinese fans, and dividing opinion on what stardom means.
articles.summary: Fang Taozi, an AI actress starring in the short drama The Laid-off Girl, has a growing fanbase in China, but her Cosmopolitan China cover sparked a row over sidelining human talent.

cover.alt: A smiling young woman, the AI-generated actress Fang Taozi

blocks.text: In the fast-paced realm of Chinese entertainment, a new star is rising with myriad onscreen gigs popping up left, right, and centre… and she doesn’t even need to sleep. Meet Fang Taozi, an AI-generated virtual actress who has been steadily building a fervent fanbase across Chinese social media. With hyper-realistic features, a carefully curated persona, and an aesthetic that perfectly captures the Gen Z zeitgeist, Fang Taozi represents the cutting edge of digital celebrity—for good and bad.

blocks.alt: RADII talks about Fang Taozi, the AI-generated actress that's recently on the Cover of Cosmopolitan China.
blocks.caption: (Left) Fang Taozi in a hyper-realistic, “a day in the life” style “photo.” Image via Vietnam.vn. (Right) Fang Taozi perfectly suited for a digital ad campaign. Image via IG/Concall.online.

blocks.text: Fans seem to be hooked on her flawless visuals and the fascinating narrative of her “life,” all propelled by her leading role in the AI short drama The Laid-off Girl (被裁掉的女孩). Unlike human idols, Fang Taozi never gets caught in scandals (that are real, at least), never ages, and can seamlessly transition between high-fashion shoots and complex CGI acting roles. While not the first AI idol, she’s the current ultimate blank canvas for digital creators, embodying a flawless yet accessible charm that resonates with an audience that’s growing frightingly fast.

blocks.alt: RADII talks about Fang Taozi, the AI-generated actress that's recently on the Cover of Cosmopolitan China.
blocks.caption: AI “actress” Fang Taozi in a digitally rendered photoshoot. Images via IG.Concall.online.
Feng as the lead in AI short drama The Laid-off Girl (被裁掉的女孩). Image via YouTube.

blocks.text: However, her rapid ascent hasn’t been without friction. The virtual star recently found herself at the center of a fiery internet debate after appearing on the cover of Cosmopolitan China. While some praised the magazine for embracing the future of fashion and technology, others were fiercely critical. The controversy primarily centers on the displacement of real human talent. Critics argue that giving a prestigious magazine cover to an algorithm sidelines flesh-and-blood models and actresses who work tirelessly for such recognition.

blocks.caption: Cosmopolitan China’s cover feature with Fang. Image via ATV News Online.

blocks.text: Furthermore, Fang Taozi’s presence amplifies ongoing conversations about unattainable beauty standards. Her literally mathematically perfect face and body present an idealized standard that no human can match, potentially fueling body image issues among her young followers.

blocks.caption: The AI-generated “actress” Fang Taozi with her AI-generated… friends? Coworker? BF? Images via Xiaohongshu.

blocks.text: As the boundary between reality and digital creation blurs, Fang Taozi stands as a polarizing figure. Is she a testament to human innovation, or a problematic reflection of our obsession with perfection? Catch Feng Taozi in AI-generated action in the video:
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/fang-taozi-ai-actress-cosmopolitan-china

articles.headline: L’EPFL dresse la première carte fine des lipides du cerveau
articles.dek: News · 29 septembre 2026
articles.summary: Grâce à l’imagerie par spectrométrie de masse, l’EPFL a cartographié 172 lipides dans le cerveau de la souris et défini 539 territoires chimiques baptisés « lipizones ».

cover.alt: Coupe coronale colorée d’un cerveau de souris

blocks.text: Le cerveau n’est pas seulement un réseau de neurones et de connexions électriques. Il est aussi un organe profondément structuré par ses lipides, ces molécules qui composent les membranes cellulaires, la myéline, les axones, les dendrites et les synapses. Une étude publiée dans Nature par des équipes de l’EPFL en offre aujourd’hui une cartographie inédite chez la souris.

Les chercheurs ont analysé le cerveau adulte à l’aide d’une technique d’imagerie par spectrométrie de masse, capable de localiser des molécules à très haute résolution. Ils ont ainsi mesuré la distribution de 172 lipides dans 109 coupes cérébrales, couvrant l’ensemble du volume du cerveau. Cette approche a permis d’identifier 539 territoires biochimiques distincts, que l’équipe appelle des « lipizones ».

Ces lipizones ne reproduisent pas simplement l’anatomie connue du cerveau. Elles révèlent une organisation chimique fine, liée aux types cellulaires, à la connectivité et à l’architecture fonctionnelle des régions cérébrales. L’étude met notamment en évidence une nouvelle forme d’hétérogénéité des oligodendrocytes, les cellules impliquées dans la formation de la myéline, ainsi qu’une zonation biochimique des ventricules cérébraux.

Autre résultat marquant: cette architecture lipidique n’est pas figée. Chez des souris gestantes, les chercheurs observent une activation métabolique de la substance blanche et un remodelage spécifique du cortex, particulièrement marqué dans la couche 4.

L’atlas, accessible en ligne, constitue désormais une ressource de référence pour explorer le rôle des lipides dans le développement, le fonctionnement et les maladies du cerveau. Il rappelle que pour comprendre le cerveau, il faut aussi cartographier sa chimie.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/lepfl-dresse-la-premiere-carte-fine-des-lipides-du-cerveau/
Cover image: Syed07 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

articles.headline: From Sichuan’s peaks to city streets: Adidas’s Shanchuanli pitch
articles.dek: Adidas’s new China outdoor identity gets a mountain launch, and eight standalone stores.
articles.summary: Adidas launched Shanchuanli, its new China name for outdoor wear, with a Sichuan summit challenge, horseriding and archery, and plans eight standalone stores while TERREX stays technical.

cover.alt: A man in outdoor clothing walking across a grassy mountain slope

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Adidas breathed life into Shanchuanli’s broad outdoor positioning at a recent launch event
• Shanchuanli expands Adidas’s appeal across competitive sport, recreational exploration and urban wear, while TERREX retains its technical role
• Adidas plans to open an initial eight standalone Shanchuanli stores

In July, Adidas announced it would be giving its outdoor line, TERREX, a new identity for the China market. The new name would be Shanchuanli (山川里) – a summing up of place, and of outdoorism as a lifestyle. Their recent Sichuan launch event tells us more about what Adidas wants Shanchuanli to be, and what it plans for the future.

The launch was experiential, with close to 100 guests and the options of a 4,000-metre summit challenge and horseriding. Archery was also involved, but those after a slower day could paint, learn to identify wild mushrooms or take a plant walk.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/这群人，让山川里有了自己的版本_2_adidas_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: shanchuanli
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/adidas

blocks.text: Guests showed as much range as the activities on offer. Olympic snowboarder Su Yiming (苏翊鸣) was there to represent competitive sport, while chef Shanyeli de Hengheng (山野里的哼哼) and botanist Gu Yourong (顾有容) brought food and nature into the mix.

All of this ties into what Shanchuanli is doing that TERREX couldn’t – it’s becoming a lifestyle brand. Adidas wants it to cover everything from competitive outdoor sport and recreational exploration to clothing worn around the city.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/这群人，让山川里有了自己的版本_5_adidas_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/adidas

blocks.text: TERREX isn’t done for. It will remain a technical marker within the new identity, but it’s there to give the expanded lifestyle proposition performance credibility. The approach also turns outdoor consumers into a much broader category. Someone painting in the mountains, examining plants or eating local food belongs alongside the athlete pushing for those high peaks.

Adidas now plans to carry that into retail. An initial eight standalone Shanchuanli stores will open across China, with the first disclosed locations including Tianjin MixC and Beijing Heshenghui. A full-category outdoor lifestyle concept store is scheduled to reach Changchun Eurasia in November.
The Dao view: A bigger tent for the outdoors

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/这群人，让山川里有了自己的版本_1_adidas_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/adidas

blocks.text: Performance gives outdoor brands credibility, but lifestyle gives them scale. Shanchuanli lets Adidas keep TERREX’s technical reputation while selling outdoor clothing across many more occasions. A jacket can move from a mountain trail to a weekday commute, and now new customers can enter through sport, food, nature or fashion.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/news/shanchuanli-adidas-launch-china/

articles.headline: The Childhood Objects Every Chinese Kid in the 2000s Knew
articles.dek: Pencil cases, lock diaries and Tamagotchis: the stuff of a pre-smartphone Chinese childhood.
articles.summary: Before smartphones, Chinese kids in the 2000s expressed themselves through gadget-packed pencil cases, lockable diaries, autograph books and Tamagotchis, a whole childhood ecosystem.

cover.alt: A handwritten page from a Chinese classmate autograph book

blocks.text: If you went to primary school in China in the early 2000s, there is a good chance you remember the same strange collection of objects: oversized plastic pencil cases, tiny diaries with combination locks, decorated classmate autograph books, Tamagotchis, magnetic construction toys, colorful water beads… the list goes on.

They were ordinary things, but together they formed a kind of childhood ecosystem. Before smartphones gave children mobile games, private spaces, digital pets, and endless entertainment, these little tangible objects did all of that themselves.

The pencil case was perhaps the most obvious example. It was never just something to put pencils and erasers in. These hard-shell plastic cases of the era came in elaborate, sometimes absurdly multifunctional designs, with buttons, sliding compartments, secret drawers, and even built-in sharpeners. Designs were also heavily gendered: pink, purple, and cartoon characters for girls; blue, racing cars, and robots for boys.

The cases became tiny expressions of personality. Your stationery could tell everyone who you were before you had a social media profile. A favorite cartoon character on a pencil case was also an early form of what we might now call IP—or otaku—culture, and the same was true of diary designs.

For many girls in particular, a diary with a tiny mechanical lock was one of the first objects that felt genuinely private. Some came with little keys, while others used three-digit combination locks. Anime characters such as Shugo Chara! were particularly popular motifs.

The funny thing is that many children had no real idea what they were protecting themselves from. As adults, some now joke that they spent so much effort choosing a password that they eventually forgot it themselves.

There is something almost poetic about that. We set up passwords to keep adults away from our childhood thoughts, only to grow up and become the adults who could no longer access those thoughts ourselves.

School memories were also stored collectively in the 同学录 (classmate autograph book). At the end of primary school, friends would pass these books around, filling in questions about their favorite food, hobbies, dreams, and impressions of one another. Pages were covered with stickers, glitter, drawings, and sometimes photographs.

Long before Instagram Stories or group chats, this was one of the ways children archived their friendships. And then there were the objects that existed for absolutely no practical reason other than being fun.

One favorite of its time was the 万花尺 (design ruler), a strange plastic drawing tool made from interlocking circles and holes. Put a pencil through one of the holes and move the inner gear around the outer frame, and it produces elaborate geometric patterns that look far more complicated than the simple movement required to make them. The technique is based on mathematical curves, but to a child, it was essentially magic.

Magnetic sticks offered another kind of low-tech fascination. Small magnetic rods and metal or plastic balls could be connected into towers, cubes, and increasingly ambitious structures. They were almost like a child’s introduction to construction, geometry, and spatial thinking, without anyone calling it educational.

Moreover, Barbie offered a different kind of open-ended play. The doll itself was only the beginning. Children changed her clothes, gave her makeovers, invented relationships between characters, and constructed elaborate stories around them. The toy was effectively a tiny stage on which children could rehearse different versions of adult life. And then there was the object that took that same idea into the digital world: Tamagotchi.

First released in Japan in 1996, Tamagotchi became a global phenomenon, with a second boom in the mid-2000s when the Tamagotchi Connection series became especially popular among children. In China, Tamagotchis and inexpensive imitations became a childhood craze, giving children a tiny digital pet to feed, clean, and care for before smartphones made virtual companionship commonplace.

Some of the strangest childhood objects were less sophisticated. 水宝宝 (water babies), often sold as colorful water-absorbing beads, were tiny polymer balls that expanded dramatically when placed in water. Children collected them in different colors and watched them grow.

They were also responsible for a surprising number of household disasters. Some children poured them down sinks or toilets, where the beads could expand and cause blockages. In other words, even our childhood toys occasionally came with a built-in plumbing lesson.

And finally, there were the completely ridiculous prank toys: fake electronic chewing gum, shocking gadgets, fake insects, novelty toys shaped like toilets, and pencil cases designed to look like something they absolutely should not look like.

blocks.caption: Ask a friend (or enemy) if they wanted a stick of gum, and they’d get quite a shock instead.

blocks.text: Looking back, these objects made us draw, build, write, care for the people around us, and even care for imaginary pets, rather than simply scroll through algorithmically recommended content. Maybe that is why, decades later, a ridiculous pink pencil case or a forgotten Tamagotchi can still feel like home.
All images via Instagram/bunnyykawaii.
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/childhood-objects-every-chinese-kid-in-the-2000s-knew

articles.headline: Une toxine fongique met les usines à protéines des cellules en pause
articles.dek: News · 29 septembre 2026
articles.summary: L’Université de Berne a identifié NT-2, une toxine du champignon Fusarium sporotrichioides qui freine fortement les ribosomes, ces usines qui fabriquent les protéines des cellules.

cover.alt: Spores et filaments d’un champignon Fusarium vus au microscope

blocks.text: Une équipe de l’Université de Berne a identifié une toxine fongique aux effets surprenants sur les cellules humaines. Baptisée NT-2, cette mycotoxine produite par le champignon pathogène Fusarium sporotrichioides est capable de ralentir fortement la production de protéines, un processus vital assuré par les ribosomes.

Les ribosomes sont souvent décrits comme les « usines à protéines » de la cellule. Ils lisent les instructions génétiques et assemblent les protéines nécessaires à la croissance, à la réparation des tissus, à l’immunité et à presque toutes les fonctions biologiques. Quand cette production est déréglée, elle peut contribuer à des maladies comme le cancer, certains troubles du développement ou des infections virales.

Pour mieux comprendre ces mécanismes, les chercheurs bernois ont développé une méthode de criblage reproduisant la production de protéines humaines en dehors de cellules vivantes. Cette approche permet d’éviter les effets parasites liés à la toxicité globale des substances testées. En analysant environ 28’000 composés, l’équipe a repéré NT-2 comme un inhibiteur particulièrement intéressant.

Grâce à la cryo-microscopie électronique, menée avec le Cryo-EM Knowledge Hub de l’ETH Zurich, les scientifiques ont observé que NT-2 se fixe au centre peptidyl-transférase du ribosome humain 60S, une zone essentielle à l’assemblage des protéines. La toxine semble aussi pousser certains ribosomes vers un état inactif, proche d’une mise en sommeil.

L’étude, réalisée avec la Biomolecular Screening Facility de l’EPFL, ne transforme pas NT-2 en médicament. Elle montre plutôt comment une toxine environnementale peut servir d’outil pour explorer le fonctionnement intime des ribosomes. À long terme, ces connaissances pourraient aider à développer de nouvelles stratégies thérapeutiques capables de moduler finement la production de protéines.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/une-toxine-fongique-met-les-usines-a-proteines-des-cellules-en-pause/
Cover image: Taragui / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

articles.headline: Alo announces eight Greater China stores after promising Tmall debut
articles.dek: After a strong Tmall debut, Alo takes its yoga wear offline with eight boutiques.
articles.summary: After a Tmall debut it says made over RMB10 million in the first minute, Alo plans eight boutiques across seven Greater China cities for 2027, plus a Hong Kong flagship.

cover.alt: An architectural rendering of a white Alo store building on a city street

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Alo plans eight new boutiques across seven Greater China cities, alongside a previously announced Hong Kong flagship
• The rollout follows its August Tmall launch, which Alo says generated more than RMB10 million (about US$1.5 million) in first-minute sales
• Alo wants the stores to build community, but has yet to confirm which facilities or activities each location will offer

Last month, Alo (爱洛) entered the Chinese market through an online-first strategy. Tmall was their platform. Now, ahead of expectations, they’re taking business from screen to street with plans for eight boutique stores in key cities throughout the Greater China market..

Openings are planned for 2027. Shanghai will get two stores, at Zhangyuan and HKRI Taikoo Hui. Six other cities will get one each. That’s Hong Kong, Beijing, Macau, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, and a Chengdu flagship. A previously announced Hong Kong flagship at K11 MUSEA is due to open this autumn in addition to the eight new boutiques.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ALO线下门店，即将开启_1_ALO爱洛_来自小红书网页版.jpg

blocks.text: Alo is calling these stores ‘Sanctuaries.’ They’re spaces for people to practice yoga, shop, and engage in wellness activities. In the US, Alo stores often have cafés and hang-out spaces, so you can safely assume these Sanctuaries will have that too.

Community makes the foundation of activewear in China and Alo says the stores will be social spaces connected to its online channels. That puts community at the centre of its pitch to Chinese shoppers, in a market where fierce competition in a number of well-established brands, all pursuing the same premium activewear customer.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ALO线下门店，即将开启_10_ALO爱洛_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Alo stores

blocks.text: The Dao view: Alo is moving fast into a crowded market

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ALO线下门店，即将开启_7_ALO爱洛_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Alo stores

blocks.text: It’s common for brands to enter the Chinese market on an e-commerce platform. Doing so means they can test demand before sinking costs into physical stores.

Alo launched on Tmall about a month before they announced this spread of new stores. That’s fast work, but Alo have reason to be confident. They say the Tmall flagship took more than RMB10 million (about US$1.5 million) in sales during its first minute.

The backdrop to their confidence is a market heating up. Domestic competitors are ramping up openings, and foreign rivals in NikeSKIMS and Vuori are competing for launch space in a market dominated by industry giant Lululemon. Alo’s speedy transition from online to offline looks a lot like a brand striking while the iron is hot.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/news/alo-china-stores/

articles.headline: A Crumbling Tradition? Why Gen Z Aren’t Buying Mooncakes Anymore
articles.dek: Health-conscious and thrifty, young Chinese are skipping the calorie-heavy festival treat.
articles.summary: Mooncake sales are slumping as health-minded, cost-conscious Gen Z still celebrate the Mid-Autumn Festival but skip the sugary pastries and pricey gift boxes.

cover.alt: Workers in a bakery tending trays of freshly baked mooncakes

blocks.text: The Mid-Autumn Festival is synonymous with family, lanterns, and, traditionally, mooncakes. But this year, the iconic pastry is facing a tough crowd: Generation Z. Sales data from recent years shows a noticeable slump in the mooncake market. The primary culprit? A seismic shift in how young Chinese consumers prioritize health and spending.

blocks.alt: RADII talks about how Gen Z are no longer buying Mooncakes for Mid-Autumn Festival due to high in sugar and expensive prices.
blocks.caption: Image via Quartz.

blocks.text: Traditionally, mooncakes are dense, calorie-heavy treats loaded with oil and sugar. For today’s wellness-obsessed youth who meticulously track their daily intake, a single slice of a traditional lotus seed paste mooncake feels like a dietary betrayal. Young people are still eager to celebrate the festival’s “sense of ceremony,” but they just don’t want to eat the calorie bombs.

blocks.alt: RADII talks about how Gen Z are no longer buying Mooncakes for Mid-Autumn Festival due to high in sugar and expensive prices.
blocks.caption: Image via Asian Inspirations.

blocks.text: Beyond health, the exorbitant cost of luxury mooncake gift boxes—once a status symbol for corporate gifting—no longer resonates with pragmatic younger buyers. Gen Z is prioritizing personal consumption over flashy gifting, refusing to drop a “pretty penny” on elaborate packaging that eventually ends up in the trash. As the industry notes, self-consumption is now surpassing gifting.

blocks.alt: RADII talks about how Gen Z are no longer buying Mooncakes for Mid-Autumn Festival due to high in sugar and expensive prices.
blocks.caption: Images via Instagram/precious.bake.

blocks.text: To survive this changing tide, heritage bakeries are scrambling to innovate. We are seeing a surge in low-sugar, low-fat alternatives, unexpected savory flavors, and trendy IP collaborations meant to entice the youth back. Whether this pivot will be enough to turn the tide remains to be seen, but one thing is clear: for Gen Z, tradition is great, but it shouldn’t come with a sugar crash or an empty wallet.
Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/gen-z-canceling-the-mooncake

articles.headline: Une nouvelle carte révèle comment le cerveau organise le mouvement
articles.dek: News · 29 septembre 2026
articles.summary: L’équipe de Silvia Arber à Bâle a divisé le cortex moteur de la souris en 16 sous-régions, chacune définie par ses connexions, à partir de 547 expériences de traçage neuronal.

cover.alt: Une souris de laboratoire tenue dans une main gantée de bleu
cover.credit: Photo: Rama / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0 fr)

blocks.text: Comment le cerveau transforme-t-il une intention en mouvement coordonné? Une équipe menée par la neuroscientifique Silvia Arber, au Biozentrum de l’Université de Bâle et au Friedrich Miescher Institute, apporte une réponse plus précise grâce à une nouvelle carte du cortex moteur de la souris.

Jusqu’ici, cette région du cerveau était souvent divisée en grandes zones, notamment un cortex moteur primaire et un cortex moteur secondaire. La nouvelle étude, publiée dans Cell, révèle une organisation beaucoup plus fine. En analysant 547 expériences de traçage neuronal, les chercheurs ont identifié 16 sous-régions distinctes, chacune définie par son propre réseau de connexions avec d’autres régions cérébrales.

Cette architecture suit deux grands axes. D’arrière en avant, les régions passent de circuits davantage liés aux informations sensorielles, comme le toucher ou la position du corps, vers des circuits associés à la planification et à la prise de décision. Latéralement, l’organisation reflète en partie les différentes zones du corps, du tronc et des membres jusqu’au visage et à la bouche.

L’étude montre aussi que les cortex moteurs primaire et secondaire pourraient fonctionner davantage en parallèle qu’en hiérarchie stricte. Tous deux envoient des signaux coordonnés vers le tronc cérébral et la moelle épinière, deux relais essentiels pour l’exécution des mouvements.

Cette carte constitue un nouvel outil de référence pour les neurosciences. Elle devrait permettre de mieux aligner les données entre laboratoires et de comparer l’organisation du cortex moteur entre espèces, y compris chez l’humain. À terme, elle pourrait aussi aider à comprendre des maladies touchant les circuits moteurs et frontaux, comme la sclérose latérale amyotrophique ou certaines formes de démence.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/mapping-how-the-brain-organizes-movement/
Cover image: Rama / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0 fr)

articles.headline: Yili wants to be China’s holiday companion for all 13 days
articles.dek: Yili puts Shen Teng and Li Xian on milk cartons for every day of a 13-day break.
articles.summary: Yili’s holiday ad puts actors Shen Teng and Li Xian’s faces on milk cartons carried through a dozen leisure scenes, pitching milk for all 13 days of the stretched Golden Week.

cover.alt: A Yili campaign poster with a cartoon milk mascot and actor Li Xian

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Three days of annual leave can give Chinese workers a 13-day break spanning Mid-Autumn Festival and the National Day holiday
• Yili places its milk across more than a dozen leisure scenarios to extend the product beyond breakfast and family consumption
• The campaign develops an idea from previous Yili campaigns

If Chinese employees take three days of annual leave between Mid-Autumn Festival and Golden Week they can string together 13 straight days off. Yili (伊利) wants them drinking milk for the whole stretch.

As always, the Chinese dairy giant is getting the message across with its characteristic humour. It has hired actors Shen Teng (沈腾) and Li Xian (李现) and director Zhang Dapeng (张大鹏) for a campaign film that follows Li and Shen through more than a dozen possible holiday activities.

The funny part is that the actors appear only as faces on Yili milk cartons, the cartons held in the hands of people doing everything from going to gigs, cycling and gaming to live music or mountain climbing.

Yili is calling itself the consumer’s jiaqi dazi (假期搭子), or ‘holiday companion’. The term dazi usually describes a person, someone you rope into various activities and pastimes. The term gives Yili an element of cultural relevance and the advert levity.

Unusual pairings is an idea that Yili has used in a previous campaign film, New Year’s Good Companion, also directed by Zhang Dapeng. It was based around the concept that holiday gift giving can be a headache, then positioned Yili as an easy addition to whatever gifts consumers were already buying.
The Dao view: from gift companion to holiday companion

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/现～在就晒出你心中最好吃的城市！_1_伊利_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.alt: Yili holiday companion
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/伊利

blocks.text: Yili is broadening its appeal from a position of strong familiarity. They can do this because they’re already a household name and therefore don’t need to spend time explaining the product. That gives Yili room for creative freedom.

It also gives Yili a way to create more reasons to buy familiar products. Milk is conventionally associated with breakfast and family households. Placing it at hotpot tables, campsites and gaming sessions asks consumers to imagine it in a much wider range of situations. Carrying milk to a gig or up a mountain is certainly more comic than credible, but that’s Yili’s style.
Source: DAO Insights — https://daoinsights.com/news/yili-holiday-companion/

articles.headline: The Legacy of Pioneering Chinese Punk Musician He Yong
articles.dek: Remembering the “Garbage Dump” rocker, one of the Three Heroes of Moyan, who died at 57.
articles.summary: He Yong, whose only album Garbage Dump made him one of the Three Heroes of Moyan, died at 57; his fade after a 1996 blacklisting mirrored the fortunes of Chinese rock.

cover.alt: Black-and-white photographs of punk musician He Yong performing

blocks.text: In 1994, He Yong released Garbage Dump, the only album of his career. It arrived during rock music’s golden decade in China, and alongside Dou Wei and Zhang Chu, He Yong became part of what fans still call the “Three Heroes of Moyan” (魔岩三杰), the golden trio of Chinese rock.

That same December, the Three Heroes of Moyan and Tang Dynasty performed together at Hong Kong Coliseum, a landmark moment in Chinese rock history. The show sold out, drawing nearly 10,000 people; among them were some of the biggest celebrities of the time, like Faye Wong, Jacky Cheung, and Andy Lau. The scale of frenzy was unlike anything the scene had seen before, much like Beatlemania’s arrival in America.

At that time, the media and the rock scene alike saw the concert as Chinese rock’s first step onto the international stage, and a future too bright to fully picture. In hindsight, that promise never arrived. Like He Yong’s quiet fade into the sidelines, rock in China suffered much of the same fate. The next time He Yong made headlines was decades later, when he passed away at 57 on September 1st of this year.

In 1996, He Yong was blacklisted after making a controversial remark during a performance. Scattered shows followed over the years, but none on a stage as grand as Hong Kong’s, and none that returned him to the spotlight. While the rest of the trio kept building their careers, He Yong slipped out of the public view. In the decades that followed, mental health struggles and legal troubles pulled him further away from the world of punk.

Still, it didn’t stop nearly all of China’s alternative music scene from paying tribute this week, sharing old photos and fond memories. Words from different people seemed to converge on the same idea, remembering him as a kind, fierce, and fearless artist, an idealist pure of heart.

blocks.alt: One of China's first punk musician, He Yong, dies at 57, RADII explores his music career and impact on Chinese rock history.
blocks.caption: Filming the music video for “Garbage Dump.” Image via Gao Yuan, a well-known photographer in China’s early rock scene.

blocks.text: Garbage Dump held only ten tracks, but each one is a masterclass in poetry and social observation. His best-known song, the title track, was written in 1989; the lyrics point out society’s meaningless quarreling, people’s lack of compassion, and the refusal of ideological reform:
The world we live in is Akin to a garbage dump People are like insects, Fighting with each other We eat our conscience, And shit out ideology.
He Yong also took aim at China’s widening wealth gap, pointing out that while the elite few have the freedom of choice, the ordinary and impoverished do not:
Some are trying to lose weight While others are starving to death

The bleakness of “Garbage Dump” stands in sharp contrast with “Bell Drum Towers,” where He Yong recalls his childhood in Beijing hutongs. It’s a nostalgic longing for the past rather than a rage against the present. At the 2004 Helan Mountains Rock Music Festival, after performing the song live, he told the crowd: “The Bell Drum Towers hasn’t changed. It’s we who’ve all grown up”

The album was originally to be titled The Qilin Diary. In Chinese mythology, the qilin is a benevolent, chimera-like creature symbolizing good fortune, prosperity, and kindness, one still found today as a stone statue, guarding offices, homes, and doorways. In the album liner notes, He Yong wrote this passage:

blocks.alt: One of China's first punk musician, He Yong, dies at 57, RADII explores his music career and impact on Chinese rock history.
blocks.caption: Images via Gao Yuan.

blocks.text: I imagine He Yong saw himself in that qilin, waiting for a wind that would carry the promise of freedom and true prosperity.

The album’s two working titles seem to point in two distinctly opposite directions, though their content remains the same. Garbage Dump paints an explicit and unapologetic portrait of 90s China, critical with a vengeance. But The Qilin Diary suggests an undercurrent of idealism, where the garbage dump is shrouded in hope. The same tension runs through the record, and He Yong’s voice shifts between a childlike melody and raw, unrestrained screaming.

In a 2004 interview, He Yong was described as an angry young man. He responded with: “There is actually love in my anger.” It’s hard to doubt that underneath all his acts of rebellion sat a genuine love and longing for freedom and equality.
May He Yong rest in peace and soar free like a qilin.

blocks.alt: One of China's first punk musician, He Yong, dies at 57, RADII explores his music career and impact on Chinese rock history.
blocks.caption: He Yong and Jiang Xin, musician and writer. Image via DJ Zhang Youdai.

blocks.text: Source: RADII — https://radii.co/article/the-legacy-of-pioneering-chinese-punk-musician-he-yong

articles.headline: Un médicament aide les cellules de la vessie à déloger les bactéries cachées
articles.dek: News · 29 septembre 2026
articles.summary: L’EPFL montre que l’OM-89, vendu sous le nom d’Uro-Vaxom, renforce les lysosomes des cellules de la vessie pour en déloger les bactéries E. coli qui s’y cachent.

cover.alt: Bactéries E. coli en forme de bâtonnets vues au microscope électronique
cover.credit: Photo: Eric Erbe and Christopher Pooley (USDA ARS) / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

blocks.text: Les infections urinaires récidivantes restent un problème fréquent et difficile à traiter. L’une des raisons est que certaines bactéries, notamment les souches uropathogènes d’Escherichia coli, peuvent se réfugier à l’intérieur des cellules de la vessie. Protégées de nombreuses défenses immunitaires et parfois moins accessibles aux antibiotiques, elles peuvent survivre puis relancer l’infection après la fin du traitement.

Une étude menée à l’EPFL et publiée dans PLOS Pathogens apporte une piste intéressante. Les chercheurs ont étudié l’effet d’OM-89, un médicament déjà commercialisé sous le nom Uro-Vaxom® pour la prévention des infections urinaires récidivantes. Jusqu’ici, son action était surtout comprise comme une stimulation générale de l’immunité innée.

Les nouveaux résultats suggèrent un mécanisme plus direct. OM-89 agit sur les cellules épithéliales de la vessie elles-mêmes, en renforçant leurs voies lysosomales. Les lysosomes sont de petits compartiments cellulaires capables de dégrader des matériaux indésirables, y compris des bactéries internalisées. En activant cette machinerie, le traitement aide les cellules à mieux éliminer les E. coli cachées.

L’étude montre aussi qu’OM-89 augmente la quantité d’antibiotique qui pénètre dans les cellules infectées. Cette double action pourrait donc améliorer l’efficacité des traitements: d’un côté, la cellule détruit mieux les bactéries; de l’autre, l’antibiotique atteint plus facilement les microbes qui échappaient jusque-là à son action.

Les auteurs restent prudents: ces résultats proviennent de modèles précliniques et ne modifient pas l’usage approuvé du médicament. Mais ils renforcent l’idée qu’une stratégie efficace contre les infections récidivantes pourrait ne pas viser uniquement la bactérie. Elle pourrait aussi aider les tissus infectés à réactiver leurs propres capacités de défense.
Source: Republic of Innovation — https://republic-of-innovation.ch/un-medicament-aide-les-cellules-de-la-vessie-a-deloger-les-bacteries-cachees/
Cover image: Eric Erbe and Christopher Pooley (USDA ARS) / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

articles.headline: Chagee teams up with CLOT for a matcha-focused collaboration
articles.dek: Chagee and Edison Chen’s CLOT turn matcha drinks into a peel-and-win collectable.
articles.summary: Chagee and Edison Chen’s CLOT launched three matcha drinks with peel-back cups that reveal dragon motifs and prizes, with more than 200,000 winning cups in circulation.

cover.alt: A green promotional poster for Chagee’s matcha drinks with CLOT

blocks.text: Key takeaways
• Chagee and CLOT launched three matcha drinks with peel-back packaging that reveals co-branded motifs and potential prizes
• Badges, blind boxes and more than 200,000 winning cups turn product sampling into a collectable experience
• Despite CLOT’s previous HEYTEA partnership, Chagee differentiates its campaign through interactive packaging and spokesperson Lin Yi.

Chagee have teamed up with much-hyped Hong Kong man of fashion Edison Chen. He’s the eye behind CLOT, the brand that launched the highly popular Chinese-style Adidas jacket. He was also part of a big-hit HEYTEA collaboration (but let’s not remind Chagee of that).

This collaboration centres on a range of matcha drinks. Actor Lin Yi (林一) fronts the packaging on a trio of vanilla, jasmine, and peach-oolong varieties. Peeling that packaging away reveals CLOT’s pale-green geometrics and dragon motifs.

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/CHAGEE×CLOT全新抹茶系列，今日上新！_4_CHAGEE霸王茶姬_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/CHAGEE霸王茶姬

blocks.text: It’s also where a prize mechanic begins. More than 200,000 winning cups are in circulation, offering customers the chance to claim branded rugs, insulated flasks or drink vouchers. A linked mini-programme promises further prizes.

Lin Yi has been a brand friend since Jan 2025. Now he’s been bumped up to matcha-series spokesperson (抹茶系列代言人). His first job was announcing to customers that they should peel back that packaging – all done through his Weibo account to solid levels of engagement.

Incentives are also built into the purchasing process. Selected single-drink sets include one of three random metal badges. Customers buying designated two-drink sets receive a blind box containing either a badge set or a plush accessory. But is this enough to stand out?
The Dao view: Differentiation is key here

blocks.src: https://daoinsights.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/9月16日起，撕杯有惊喜🎁_2_CHAGEE霸王茶姬_来自小红书网页版.jpg
blocks.caption: Images: Rednote/CHAGEE霸王茶姬
